A.q: A 46-year-old man who has drunk heavily for 20 years has six months of worsening breathlessness on exertion and orthopnea (breathlessness lying flat). The apical impulse is displaced laterally and a third heart sound (an early diastolic sound just after the second heart sound) is heard. Echocardiogram shows dilated, thin-walled ventricles with an ejection fraction of 25%, and coronary angiography shows no significant narrowing. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy shows a thick, often asymmetric septum with a small cavity and a normal or high ejection fraction, not thin, dilated walls with an ejection fraction of 25%.
Restrictive cardiomyopathy keeps a near-normal cavity size and systolic function with stiff walls and big atria. Dilated, thin walls with poor squeeze are the dilated pattern instead.
Stress (Takotsubo) cardiomyopathy is a transient regional weakness of the mid and apical segments after a stressor, mostly in postmenopausal women, not a slow global dilation over months.

Correct. Dilation and impaired contraction without severe coronary disease or pressure or volume overload define dilated cardiomyopathy, and long-term excess alcohol is one of its named causes. The displaced apical impulse and third heart sound fit a dilated, volume-overloaded ventricle.

A.q: In the low likelihood Wells category, what happens after a negative D-dimer?
opts: The test is repeated in a week
Repeat imaging applies after a negative ultrasound in high likelihood patients. A negative D-dimer in the low category ends the work-up.
Venography is invasive and largely replaced by ultrasound. A negative D-dimer in the low category ends the work-up.
Correct. In the low likelihood Wells category a negative D-dimer ends the work-up, since the test is sensitive enough to rule out deep vein thrombosis.
Ultrasound follows a positive D-dimer, not a negative one. A negative result in the low likelihood category ends the work-up.

A.q: A 37-year-old man was treated for acute pericarditis 4 weeks ago and now feels well. A repeat electrocardiogram shows widespread T-wave inversions without ST elevation, and troponin is normal. Which best explains the tracing?
opts: With normal troponin and a known recent pericarditis, diffuse T-wave inversion fits the third stage of the pericarditis evolution.
ruled out by a stated finding
Correct. The classic evolution is widespread ST elevation with PR depression, then ST normalization with T-wave flattening, then inversion of the flattened T waves, and finally a normal tracing.
Hyperkalemia peaks the T waves rather than inverting them; this is the expected evolution of pericarditis.
Tamponade gives low voltage and electrical alternans with hemodynamic signs, not isolated T-wave inversion in a well patient.

A.q: A 66-year-old man has a story strongly suggesting constrictive pericarditis: edema, ascites, an elevated jugular venous pressure with the Kussmaul sign (a rise on inspiration). His chest radiograph shows no pericardial calcification. How should this radiograph be interpreted?
opts: Correct. Pericardial calcification is highly consistent with constriction when present, but most patients do not have it on chest radiograph, so a film without calcium cannot rule the diagnosis out.
A film without calcium does not point to restrictive cardiomyopathy; that distinction relies on echocardiography, natriuretic peptide and imaging.
It shows the cause is tamponade
Tamponade is a clinical diagnosis of fluid under pressure; a radiograph without calcium says nothing in its favor.
Most patients with constriction show no calcification, so a clear radiograph cannot exclude it.

A.q: In a stable narrow complex tachycardia, which step comes before any drug?
opts: Procainamide is reserved for atrial fibrillation with Wolff-Parkinson-White; the first step in stable narrow complex tachycardia is a vagal maneuver.
Correct. A vagal maneuver is first line for stable supraventricular (narrow complex) tachycardia, before adenosine; synchronized cardioversion is kept for instability.
Imaging does not terminate the rhythm; in a stable narrow complex tachycardia the first step is a vagal maneuver.
Synchronized cardioversion is immediate treatment only when the patient is unstable; a stable patient starts with a vagal maneuver.

opts: Correct. Left bundle branch block is usually left untreated, except symptomatic left bundle branch block with heart failure with reduced ejection fraction, which gets a biventricular pacer.
A conventional pacemaker treats slow rhythms. Resynchronizing the ventricles in this setting calls for a biventricular pacer.
Magnesium treats torsades de pointes. Symptomatic left bundle branch block with reduced ejection fraction is treated with a biventricular pacer.
Ablation destroys tissue and cannot restore left ventricular activation. A biventricular pacer resynchronizes the ventricles.

A.q: A 73-year-old man with painful blue toes and palpable pulses asks what the emboli in his toes are made of. Which answer is accurate?
opts: Correct. Atheroembolism is multiple small deposits of fibrin, platelets and cholesterol debris embolizing from proximal atherosclerotic lesions to the small vessels of skin and muscle.
A clot from the heart is a thromboembolus, the usual cause of acute limb ischemia with absent pulses. Blue toes with pulses reflect cholesterol-rich debris from plaque.
Valve vegetations are not the source named for blue toe syndrome. The debris is fibrin, platelets and cholesterol shed from proximal atherosclerotic plaques.
Air embolism is not the process described. Atheroemboli are small deposits of fibrin, platelets and cholesterol debris from proximal plaques.

A.q: Which lifestyle measures are advised for adults with cardiomyopathy?
opts: Strict bed rest and total fluid restriction
Bed rest is not the advice, and cardiac rehabilitation aims to improve exercise tolerance. The lifestyle measures are sodium restriction and alcohol cessation.
Fluid loading and a high-salt diet plan
Fluid and salt loading worsen congestion. Adults are advised to restrict sodium and stop alcohol.
Caffeine avoidance and deliberate weight gain
Neither is part of adult strategy. The lifestyle modifications are sodium restriction and alcohol cessation.
Correct. Adult lifestyle modifications are sodium restriction and alcohol cessation, alongside guideline-directed medical therapy and device therapy.

A.q: A 70-year-old woman with right-sided heart failure has atrial flutter (sawtooth flutter waves) with a ventricular rate of 140. She is alert, with a blood pressure of 124/78 and no chest pain. Which is the most appropriate initial treatment?
opts: A beta or calcium channel blocker
Correct. Hemodynamically stable atrial flutter is rate-controlled with a beta blocker or calcium channel blocker; rate control is the first goal, though harder to achieve than in fibrillation.
Adenosine is used for reentrant supraventricular tachycardia; stable flutter is rate-controlled.
Synchronized cardioversion is for unstable flutter; she is stable, so rate control comes first.
A pacemaker treats slow rhythms; flutter at 140 needs rate control with a beta blocker or calcium channel blocker.

A.q: A 68-year-old woman has crushing chest pain and breathlessness the day after her husband's funeral. She has no hypertension, diabetes or smoking history. The electrocardiogram shows ST elevation with T-wave inversion, troponin is elevated, and echocardiogram shows hypokinesis of the mid and apical segments of the left ventricle. Catheterization shows normal coronary arteries. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Correct. A postmenopausal woman after an emotional stressor, with ST elevation, raised troponin, mid and apical hypokinesis and normal coronary arteries at catheterization, has Takotsubo (stress) cardiomyopathy.
Restrictive cardiomyopathy presents late with right-sided congestion and big atria. Sudden chest pain after grief with apical hypokinesis is stress cardiomyopathy.
Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy is an inherited thickening of the septum with an outflow murmur. It does not produce transient apical hypokinesis after a stressor.
Dilated cardiomyopathy is a progressive global dilation with reduced squeeze over months, not a sudden regional apical weakness triggered by emotional stress.

A.q: A 19-year-old woman with a week of fever and myalgia now has severe breathlessness. She is cold and clammy with a blood pressure of 78/50, heart rate 128, raised jugular venous pressure and crackles throughout both lungs. Myocarditis is suspected. Which is the most appropriate next step?
opts: Exercise testing has no place in cardiogenic shock. Myocarditis this severe needs aggressive hemodynamic stabilization.

Correct. Myocarditis can present as cardiogenic shock, and although supportive care is the mainstay, treatment is directed toward the scenario and may require aggressive hemodynamic stabilization first.
She is in cardiogenic shock, a presentation of myocarditis that can be rapidly fatal. Delay is unsafe; aggressive hemodynamic stabilization comes first.
Biopsy can establish the diagnosis later, but it is not done before a patient in shock is stabilized. Aggressive hemodynamic stabilization comes first.

A.q: A 64-year-old man had an anterior myocardial infarction 3 weeks ago. He now has fever, pleuritic (worse with a deep breath) chest pain eased by sitting forward, and a friction rub (a scratchy, three-part rubbing sound) at the left sternal border. Which drug should be avoided in treating his pericarditis?
opts: Colchicine is added to aspirin for post-infarction pericarditis; it is part of the treatment, not a drug to avoid.

Correct. This is post-infarction (Dressler) pericarditis, and nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs such as ibuprofen are not given after a myocardial infarction; glucocorticoids are also avoided. Aspirin plus colchicine is used.
Aspirin is exactly the anti-inflammatory used for post-infarction pericarditis, continued from his infarction care, with colchicine added.
A proton pump inhibitor such as pantoprazole gives the gastrointestinal protection that anti-inflammatory therapy calls for; it is not avoided.

A.q: A 62-year-old woman taking metoprolol and diltiazem for palpitations has a new rhythm in which the PR interval lengthens until a QRS is dropped. She has mild fatigue. Which part of her history is a named cause of this rhythm?
opts: Fatigue is a possible symptom of the block, not its cause. Her rate-slowing medications are the named cause.
Sex is not a named cause. Beta blockers and nondihydropyridine calcium channel blockers are listed causes of Mobitz type I.
Palpitations are the reason for her drugs, not a cause of block. Her beta blocker and nondihydropyridine calcium channel blocker are named causes.
Correct. Beta blockers and nondihydropyridine calcium channel blockers, with digoxin, are named causes of Mobitz type I block, so her medication list is the first place to look.

A.q: A 68-year-old man who started amlodipine for hypertension five weeks ago has bilateral, symmetric ankle swelling without warmth, redness or tenderness. Which is the most appropriate next step?
opts: Symmetric swelling without warmth or tenderness after starting amlodipine is the classic picture of drug-induced edema, not of clot, which is usually unilateral. Imaging is not the first step.
Review the medication as the cause

Correct. Dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers such as amlodipine commonly cause edema, typically bilateral and without signs of inflammation. Recognizing drug-induced edema and reviewing the medication list is the appropriate step.
A D-dimer is a nonspecific test used when deep vein thrombosis is a real concern. With bilateral, noninflamed swelling after a new drug, the likelier explanation is the medication.
Anticoagulation treats a confirmed clot and carries bleeding risk. Bilateral swelling with no inflammation after a new calcium channel blocker points to a drug effect, so a clot is unlikely.

opts: Aspirin is an antiplatelet agent for chronic peripheral artery disease. The medical therapy for an acute arterial occlusion is anticoagulation with intravenous heparin.
Correct. The medical therapy for acute peripheral arterial occlusion is anticoagulation with intravenous heparin, started alongside an immediate vascular surgery consult.
Cilostazol is an oral antiplatelet used for chronic claudication. Acute limb ischemia is anticoagulated with intravenous heparin while surgery is arranged.
Pentoxifylline is a xanthine derivative for chronic claudication. Acute arterial occlusion needs intravenous heparin anticoagulation and a vascular surgery consult.

opts: Defibrillation is for ventricular fibrillation and pulseless ventricular tachycardia. A slow dissociated rhythm with a pulse needs pacing.
Amiodarone suppresses tachyarrhythmias and would slow him further. Unstable complete block needs transcutaneous pacing.
Cardioversion terminates fast rhythms. Complete heart block with a rate of 32 needs pacing, not a shock.
Correct. Unstable complete heart block is treated emergently with transcutaneous pacing, pads on the chest, as a bridge to the definitive permanent pacemaker.

A.q: A 78-year-old man with diabetes and known black, shriveled toe tips now has a moist, swollen, blistered forefoot. His temperature is 39.2 C and heart rate 118. Which is the most appropriate next step?
opts: Exercise therapy is for stable claudication. A moist, blistered, infected foot with fever and tachycardia is wet gangrene, a surgical emergency.

Correct. Wet gangrene (moist, edematous, blistering tissue with bacterial infection, often clostridial) is a surgical emergency because of the risk of sepsis, unlike the dry gangrene common in peripheral artery disease.
Waiting for demarcation suits dry gangrene, which is hard, dry and clearly demarcated. Wet gangrene with fever carries a risk of sepsis and is a surgical emergency.
Antiplatelet therapy treats chronic arterial disease and cannot control infected tissue. Wet gangrene with signs of sepsis needs emergency surgical care.

A.q: A 71-year-old man hospitalized for six days with pneumonia develops swelling of the left calf. His team considers using the Wells criteria to estimate his probability of deep vein thrombosis. Which statement about applying the Wells criteria to him is accurate?
opts: A low score replaces all testing
A low score does not replace testing; it leads to a D-dimer first, and only a negative result stops the work-up. The score guides which test comes next, not whether to test.
The Wells criteria for deep vein thrombosis address suspected leg clots, with items such as calf swelling and pitting edema of the leg. Upper-extremity clots are not what this score was built for.
Meant for outpatient or emergency use

Correct. The Wells criteria are used in the outpatient and emergency department settings, not for inpatients, in whom the score is less useful. A hospitalized patient needs clinical judgment and ultrasound rather than this pathway.
The score is less useful in hospitalized patients; it is validated for outpatients and emergency department patients. Inpatients need clinical judgment and ultrasound instead of this pathway.

opts: Nodal reentry is a regular narrow tachycardia, usually in younger women without heart disease; it is not the fast phase of tachy-brady syndrome.
Ventricular fibrillation is a pulseless arrest rhythm, not a recurring run she survives; the usual fast rhythm of tachy-brady syndrome is atrial fibrillation.
Correct. Fast rhythms alternating with bradycardia and offset pauses are tachy-brady syndrome, a form of sick sinus syndrome in which the tachyarrhythmia is most commonly atrial fibrillation.
In tachy-brady syndrome the fast rhythm comes from outside the failing sinus node, most commonly atrial fibrillation.

A.q: A 65-year-old man has a painful, swollen right groin two days after a cardiac catheterization through the femoral artery. Ultrasound shows a blood-filled cavity outside the arterial wall, communicating with the lumen. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Acute limb ischemia is a sudden occlusion with a cold, pale, pulseless limb. A painful groin swelling with an extraluminal cavity is a pseudoaneurysm.
A true aneurysm involves all three layers of the vessel wall. A cavity outside the wall after needle laceration is a false aneurysm, a pseudoaneurysm.

Correct. A pseudoaneurysm is a communication between the arterial lumen and overlying connective tissue after arterial rupture; the common site is the femoral artery after cardiac catheterization, from laceration by the access needle.
Atheroembolism causes painful blue toes with palpable pulses. A post-catheterization cavity outside the arterial wall is a pseudoaneurysm.

opts: Correct. The classical strategy starts with heparin and bridges to warfarin; it is cheap and reliable but needs frequent laboratory follow-up of the international normalized ratio.

A.q: A 3-week-old infant born at 28 weeks is in the neonatal intensive care unit with a central venous catheter and parenteral nutrition. She develops feeding difficulty, tachycardia, hypotension and a new murmur, and echocardiography shows a right-sided vegetation. Which organism group is particularly tied to her risk factors?
opts: Enterococci are less common in children than adults and are not tied to neonatal lines and hyperalimentation.

Correct. Neonatal fungal endocarditis is tied to central venous catheters, hyperalimentation and neonatal intensive care or prematurity; Staphylococcus aureus and coagulase-negative staphylococci are also common.
The HACEK (Haemophilus, Aggregatibacter, Cardiobacterium, Eikenella, Kingella) group is not the neonatal catheter organism.
Viridans streptococci cause indolent disease in children over 1 year with congenital heart disease, not catheter-related neonatal infection.

A.q: A 34-year-old woman has frequent, disruptive episodes of atrioventricular nodal reentry and wants a definitive cure. Referral for which procedure is most appropriate?
opts: A pacemaker treats slow rhythms such as sick sinus syndrome; nodal reentry is cured by catheter ablation.
Correct. Catheter ablation offers a select subset of patients with nodal reentry the opportunity for a definitive cure, in over 95%.
Myectomy relieves outflow obstruction in hypertrophic cardiomyopathy; it does not treat nodal reentry.
Nodal reentry usually occurs without heart disease, in structurally normal hearts; valve surgery has no role.

A.q: Which electrical treatment is delivered for polymorphic ventricular tachycardia?
opts: Correct. Polymorphic ventricular tachycardia is never truly stable and its QRS shape keeps changing, so it is defibrillated (unsynchronized) even when a pulse is present.
Transcutaneous pacing treats slow, blocked rhythms such as Mobitz type II and complete block. Polymorphic ventricular tachycardia is treated with unsynchronized defibrillation.
Synchronized cardioversion times the shock to a consistent QRS and suits unstable monomorphic rhythm with a pulse. Polymorphic rhythm is defibrillated.
Polymorphic ventricular tachycardia is never truly stable, so there is no trial of drugs first: it is defibrillated, and an antiarrhythmic or beta blocker may be added afterward.

A.q: A 60-year-old woman has viridans streptococcal endocarditis diagnosed early, before any heart failure or abscess, and she starts appropriate antibiotics the same day. Which statement about her outlook is most accurate?
opts: A 30-40% valve replacement rate is described for enterococcal endocarditis, not early-treated viridans streptococci.
Death within weeks describes untreated acute endocarditis, not early-treated viridans streptococcal disease.
Highest mortality belongs to Staphylococcus aureus, especially on prosthetic valves.
Correct. Viridans streptococcal endocarditis has a relatively good prognosis if antibiotic treatment starts before complications occur.

A.q: Which plaque is the vulnerable, unstable type?
opts: Correct. A vulnerable plaque has a fatty core under a thin fibrous outer shell and can rupture into the bloodstream; clotting then begins at the rupture site and can go on to occlude the artery.
Calcification of the media belongs to medial calcific sclerosis. The unstable plaque of atherosclerosis has a fatty core and a thin fibrous shell.
A thick fibrous shell is the stable plaque. The vulnerable plaque is the one with a fatty core and a thin fibrous outer shell that can rupture.
The fatty streak is the earliest lesion, developing between the intima and the media. The unstable plaque has a fatty core with a thin fibrous shell.

A.q: For recurrent, colchicine-resistant pericarditis with an inflammatory phenotype, which therapy do the 2025 guidelines now support earlier in the course?
opts: Surgery is considered for frequent, highly symptomatic recurrences with effusion or for constriction; with an inflammatory phenotype, anti-interleukin-1 therapy is used earlier.
Azathioprine is a later-line immunosuppressant on the older treatment table. With an inflammatory phenotype, anakinra or rilonacept is the agent now used earlier.
Intravenous immunoglobulin is a later-line immunomodulator on the older treatment table. The 2025 guidelines move anti-interleukin-1 therapy earlier for this phenotype.

Correct. The 2025 guidelines support anti-interleukin-1 therapy (anakinra or rilonacept) earlier in the course with an inflammatory phenotype, and it is preferred for recurrent, colchicine-resistant or steroid-dependent disease.

opts: Oral, short therapy cannot sterilize a vegetation; endocarditis needs bactericidal, parenteral, prolonged therapy.
Nafcillin with rifampin belongs to directed therapy for methicillin-susceptible Staphylococcus aureus on a prosthetic valve, not empiric native valve therapy.
A single oral dose of amoxicillin is dental prophylaxis, not treatment of established endocarditis, which needs prolonged parenteral therapy.

Correct. Empiric therapy covers staphylococci, streptococci and enterococci; vancomycin plus ceftriaxone is the regimen for a subacute presentation, native valve endocarditis, or a prosthetic valve in place more than a year.

opts: Adenosine slows conduction through the atrioventricular node and is used for stable supraventricular tachycardia; it would worsen a bradycardia.
A permanent pacemaker is definitive care for chronic symptomatic bradycardia; the acute, unstable patient first gets atropine, then a temporary pacemaker.
Correct. Atropine is first line for acute, symptomatic, hemodynamically unstable bradycardia; if it fails, a temporary pacemaker follows, and chronic symptomatic disease gets a permanent pacemaker.
Amiodarone is an antiarrhythmic tried for chemical cardioversion of focal atrial tachycardia, not a drug to speed a slow heart; atropine is first line.

Procainamide prolongs the QT and is avoided in torsades. Magnesium is the first treatment.
Beta blockers are avoided because the slower rate indirectly lengthens the QT. Magnesium is given first.

A week-long global state is not the definition. The attack is a focal deficit resolving within 24 hours.
Correct. A transient ischemic attack is a focal loss of neurologic function lasting less than 24 hours; it and stroke classify a patient with carotid disease as symptomatic.

A.q: Which high-risk pediatric condition warrants endocarditis prophylaxis before qualifying procedures?
opts: A family history of valve disease
Family history is not on the high-risk list; unrepaired cyanotic congenital heart disease is.
A defect repaired years ago, no residual leak
A repair with no residual defect is high risk only in the first 6 months after repair with prosthetic material or a device; years later it does not warrant prophylaxis.

Correct. High-risk pediatric conditions include unrepaired cyanotic congenital heart disease (including palliative shunts and conduits), prosthetic valves or material, prior endocarditis, and cardiac transplant with valvulopathy.
An innocent murmur found on screening
An innocent murmur is not a high-risk condition. Unrepaired cyanotic congenital heart disease is.

A.q: A 21-year-old man collapses while playing basketball and arrives with a very fast regular tachycardia. He is alert with a blood pressure of 112/70. A vagal maneuver fails, and adenosine slows the rate to reveal an irregular rhythm with wide QRS complexes, each with a delta wave (slurred upstroke). Which is the next step?
opts: More adenosine blocks only the normal node, leaving the accessory pathway free to conduct the fibrillation at rates approaching 300.

Correct. When slowing from adenosine reveals atrial fibrillation with Wolff-Parkinson-White, intravenous procainamide is used and adenosine is never repeated: nodal blockade leaves the accessory pathway unopposed.
Atropine speeds conduction and treats unstable bradycardia; it would make a pre-excited tachycardia faster.
An oral beta blocker is too slow and, as a nodal blocker, leaves the accessory pathway unopposed; procainamide is the drug used.

A.q: A 44-year-old man with hypertrophic cardiomyopathy has chest pressure when climbing stairs. Coronary angiography performed before a planned myectomy shows normal coronary arteries. Which explanation best accounts for his exertional chest pain?
opts: His coronary arteries are normal, so plaque rupture is not the cause. The angina comes from outflow obstruction and the oxygen demand of thick muscle.
Outflow obstruction and thick muscle demand

Correct. Angina without coronary disease in hypertrophic cardiomyopathy comes from left ventricular outflow tract obstruction and the increased oxygen consumption of hypertrophied muscle, causing ischemia during exertion.
A dilated, thin-walled ventricle is dilated cardiomyopathy. In hypertrophic cardiomyopathy the ventricle is thick, and its oxygen demand plus outflow obstruction cause angina.
Pericardial inflammation is a differential for restrictive disease, not the source of exertional angina here. Outflow obstruction and hypertrophy drive it.

A.q: A 51-year-old man with dilated cardiomyopathy drinks most of a bottle of whiskey every night. He is on a beta blocker and an angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitor, his ejection fraction is 30%, and he asks whether anything he does himself could help his heart recover. Which counseling point is most accurate?
opts: Wine would be safer than spirits for him
Changing the drink does not remove the cause. Education for dilated cardiomyopathy is to remove the offending source, which here means alcohol cessation.
Only a transplant could restore function
Transplantation is kept for advanced disease unresponsive to therapy. Here the reversible cause is alcohol, and stopping it can let the heart recover on its own.
Stopping alcohol may let function recover

Correct. With long-term excess alcohol as the cause, cardiac function can recover if intake is reduced or stopped, and removing the offending source is part of patient education for dilated cardiomyopathy.
Damage is fixed once the heart dilates
Alcohol-related dilated cardiomyopathy is one cause where cardiac function can recover when drinking is reduced or halted, so the damage is not necessarily permanent.

opts: Oral rate control suits a stable patient without rapid ventricular response, not someone hypotensive and confused.
Intravenous rate control is for the stable patient with rapid ventricular response; this patient is unstable.
Three weeks of anticoagulation precedes elective outpatient cardioversion; instability needs cardioversion now.
Correct. Hemodynamically unstable atrial fibrillation (hypotension and altered mental status) is treated with synchronized cardioversion.

opts: Oral step-down does not treat persistent bacteremia; therapy stays parenteral, and infection not resolving on appropriate antibiotics is a surgical indication.
Stopping therapy in persistent bacteremia risks valve destruction and death; surgical evaluation is indicated instead.
Anticoagulation is not beneficial in native valve infection and does not clear bacteremia.
Correct. Infection not resolving with appropriate antibiotic therapy is an indication for surgery, as are heart failure from valve dysfunction, abscess and fungal infection.

A.q: A 69-year-old woman is brought in by her daughter for 2 days of new confusion. She has a fever of 38.9 °C (102.0 °F), a new murmur and conjunctival petechiae (pinpoint hemorrhages on the conjunctiva). Brain imaging shows multiple small scattered lesions without a large stroke. Which mechanism best explains her confusion?
opts: No sedating drug is described; fever, a murmur, petechiae and scattered brain lesions point to septic emboli from a vegetation.
No conduction block is described; scattered lesions with fever and a murmur point to septic emboli.
Correct. Vegetations shower septic emboli into the systemic circulation; the brain is affected (ischemic stroke, abscess, hemorrhage, meningitis), producing neurologic deficits such as confusion.
Meningitis is one cerebral complication, but scattered small lesions with a new murmur and petechiae point to septic emboli from a vegetation.

A.q: A 45-year-old man with a first deep vein thrombosis is otherwise healthy and hemodynamically stable. The plan is oral anticoagulation monotherapy with a loading phase followed by maintenance, without any injection lead-in. Which drug fits this strategy?
opts: Correct. Apixaban, a direct factor Xa inhibitor, is given as oral monotherapy with a loading dose followed by a maintenance dose, one of the three major anticoagulation strategies. Rivaroxaban follows the same pattern.
Fondaparinux is an indirect factor Xa inhibitor given by injection, so it cannot be the oral monotherapy the plan describes. Apixaban is the oral direct factor Xa inhibitor for that strategy.

Dabigatran, a direct thrombin inhibitor, is started only after about five days of parenteral therapy. It does not follow the loading-then-maintenance oral monotherapy strategy that this plan describes.
Edoxaban is an anti-Xa agent, but it also follows five days of parenteral anticoagulation rather than serving as a stand-alone oral loading strategy. Apixaban fits an oral-only plan.

opts: A transient ischemic attack causes focal neurologic deficits, not a sudden faint with a slow rate. This is a Stokes-Adams attack.
An absence seizure is a brief staring spell without collapse. Her collapse came from low cerebral blood flow during heart block.
Vasovagal syncope follows a trigger such as pain or standing, with a prodrome. A sudden faint from a blocked rhythm with a rate of 36 is a Stokes-Adams attack.
Correct. A Stokes-Adams attack is a sudden fainting spell or seizure from a rapid, temporary drop in blood flow to the brain, a recognized complication of Mobitz type II block.

opts: Correct. A regular tachycardia with one consistent, abnormally shaped P wave before each QRS, starting abruptly in someone without heart disease under increased metabolic demand, is focal atrial tachycardia.
Flutter shows sawtooth waves at 250 or more per minute, not a single abnormal P wave before each QRS at 160.
Sinus tachycardia keeps the patient's normal P-wave shape; a consistent abnormal P wave means an ectopic atrial focus.
ruled out by a stated finding

A.q: A 24-year-old man with known obstructive hypertrophic cardiomyopathy has a crescendo-decrescendo systolic murmur at the left sternal border that radiates to the suprasternal notch. At the bedside, the examiner tests how the murmur responds to changes in blood flow through the heart. Which maneuver would make his murmur louder?
opts: Passive leg raising increases preload, filling the ventricle and lessening outflow obstruction, so the murmur softens. Decreasing preload with the Valsalva maneuver makes it louder.

Correct. Anything that decreases blood flow in the heart increases the outflow obstruction and the murmur. The Valsalva maneuver and standing reduce preload, so the murmur of obstructive hypertrophic cardiomyopathy gets louder.
Rapid squatting increases preload and so reduces outflow obstruction and softens the murmur. Standing or the Valsalva maneuver, which decrease preload, make it louder.
Handgrip increases afterload, which increases blood flow in the ventricle and reduces outflow obstruction, so the murmur of obstructive hypertrophic cardiomyopathy becomes softer.

A.q: A 68-year-old man is 4 days into his recovery from a large anterior myocardial infarction when he suddenly becomes hypotensive, with distended neck veins and muffled heart sounds. Which is the most likely explanation?
opts: Constriction develops over months and does not cause sudden collapse days after an infarction.

Dressler syndrome is an inflammatory pericarditis weeks after infarction, with pain and a rub, not sudden collapse with the Beck triad (hypotension, distended neck veins, muffled heart sounds) on day 4.
Correct. Free-wall rupture after myocardial infarction is a recognized cause of tamponade, alongside acute pericarditis, iatrogenic injury, trauma, malignancy and aortic dissection.
Massive pulmonary embolism can mimic acute tamponade, but muffled heart sounds days after a large anterior infarction point to free-wall rupture filling the pericardium.

A.q: A 59-year-old man with a large pericardial effusion from metastatic cancer reports a hoarse voice, hiccups and difficulty swallowing. Which mechanism explains his hoarseness?
opts: Correct. Large effusions can cause dysphagia, nausea, hiccups, cough and hoarseness, the hoarseness from impingement of the recurrent laryngeal nerve.
Vena cava obstruction swells the face and arms; hoarseness comes from the recurrent laryngeal nerve.
The hypoglossal nerve moves the tongue and is far from the pericardium. The recurrent laryngeal nerve is impinged.
Direct invasion of the vocal cords
The effusion does not invade the larynx. It compresses the recurrent laryngeal nerve on its course through the chest.

A.q: A 78-year-old man with chronic kidney disease, pulmonary hypertension and hyponatremia is diagnosed with constrictive pericarditis. His family asks what to expect. Which statement about his long-term outlook is most accurate?

Without treatment, survival in constrictive pericarditis is low, not normal; surgery improves it.
His prognosis is as good as a young patient's
His age and comorbidities make the outlook worse than a younger, healthier patient's.
Age does not influence the outcome of surgery
Older adults carry higher morbidity and mortality with surgery, and older age itself predicts a poorer outcome.
His age and comorbidities predict a worse outcome
Correct. Older age, worse functional class and comorbidities such as renal dysfunction, pulmonary hypertension and hyponatremia are independent predictors of poor long-term outcome in constriction.

A.q: A 62-year-old man on hemodialysis has a left forearm arteriovenous fistula that was created four months ago. Last month it had a palpable thrill (a vibration felt over the access) and a soft bruit. At today's visit no thrill can be felt and no bruit is heard over the access. Which is the most appropriate next step?
opts: Warm compresses and an anti-inflammatory drug
That regimen treats superficial thrombophlebitis of a vein. A fistula without thrill or bruit has a flow problem that needs specialist evaluation, not symptomatic care.
Reassurance would miss a failing access. A working fistula carries a thrill and a soft bruit, so absence of both is abnormal and warrants prompt specialist evaluation.

Correct. A healthy fistula has a diffuse thrill and a soft bruit with systolic and diastolic components. Loss of both means the access is no longer working, so it needs prompt referral to the specialist.

opts: Computed tomography angiography is limited by contrast allergy and decreased renal function, not by a pacemaker. It is usable here if his kidneys and allergy history allow.
Correct. Magnetic resonance angiography is contraindicated with pacemakers and intracranial aneurysm clips. It is otherwise the alternative to computed tomography angiography in contrast allergy.
Conventional angiography is the invasive gold standard used to guide a planned intervention. A pacemaker does not prevent it; the pacemaker rules out magnetic resonance.

A.q: A 49-year-old man has 3 weeks of fever and night sweats. Two separate blood cultures grow Streptococcus gallolyticus, and a transesophageal echocardiogram shows an oscillating mass on the aortic valve. He has no skin, eye or kidney findings. How is his case classified under the modified Duke criteria?
opts: Possible is one major plus one minor, or three minor criteria. He has two major criteria, which is definite.
No further test is needed to classify him; two major criteria already make the diagnosis definite.

Correct. Two major criteria are met: a typical organism (Streptococcus gallolyticus) in two separate cultures and an oscillating mass on echocardiogram. Two major criteria alone establish definite endocarditis.
Two separate cultures of a typical organism and an oscillating mass are two major criteria, which confirm endocarditis rather than exclude it.

A.q: A 62-year-old woman who had a left leg deep vein thrombosis after a hip fracture ten years ago reports a heavy, aching left lower leg by evening that eases when she elevates it. Examination shows pitting edema, shiny taut skin at the ankle and brownish pigmentation. Pedal pulses are strong. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Arterial disease causes exertional cramping relieved by rest and weak pulses, and pitting edema is not its feature. Strong pulses with edema and pigmentation point to venous disease.

Correct. Progressive pitting edema with dull discomfort worse on standing, shiny taut ankle skin and brownish pigmentation after a prior deep vein thrombosis are the classic picture of chronic venous insufficiency.
Lymphedema is unilateral, lacks varicosities, and brawny hemosiderin staining is rare in it. Pitting edema with brown pigmentation after a prior clot is venous insufficiency.

Numbness and burning describe neuropathy. Varicose veins produce aching heaviness and fatigue with standing and may itch over the veins.

Hypothyroidism slows the sinus node and causes bradycardia; it does not explain a racing heart after stopping a beta blocker.

Her cancer is in remission and untreated. Her clinician judges chronic lymphedema at least as likely as deep vein thrombosis. Which test comes next by the Wells criteria?
opts: Correct. Three positive items (calf swelling, pitting edema, deep venous tenderness) give 3 points, and the likelier alternative diagnosis subtracts 2, leaving 1, a moderate likelihood. Moderate scores of 1 to 2 need a D-dimer.
Ultrasound goes first only for a high score of 3 or more. Subtracting 2 for lymphedema leaves her at 1, a moderate score that starts with a D-dimer.
Contrast ascending venography is the invasive gold standard that venous duplex ultrasound replaced. It is not an initial test for a moderate score, which begins with a D-dimer.

Home-based rehabilitation is recommended for elderly or mobility-limited patients and is not a drug. Caution in the elderly applies to diuretics and vasodilators.
Sodium restriction is a lifestyle measure, not a drug, and it is part of adult cardiomyopathy care. The medications singled out for caution in the elderly are diuretics and vasodilators.

Intravenous magnesium breaks torsades de pointes; pre-excited atrial fibrillation is treated with procainamide.
Atropine speeds conduction and is used for unstable bradycardia; it would make a pre-excited tachycardia faster, not slower.

B.q: A 24-year-old woman with chest pain and breathlessness after a recent viral illness is being evaluated for myocarditis. Her electrocardiogram shows sinus tachycardia. Which laboratory result would indicate cardiac myonecrosis?

A B-type natriuretic peptide below 100 pg/mL argues against heart failure; it is not a marker of myonecrosis. Elevated troponin is.

The erythrocyte sedimentation rate may be elevated in myocarditis, and in either case it does not indicate myonecrosis. Troponin is the marker of heart muscle injury.

B.q: A 55-year-old man has a positive D-dimer during evaluation of calf pain two weeks after a bicycle crash with extensive bruising. He asks why his clinician says the result cannot confirm a clot. Which explanation is accurate?
opts: It rises only with pulmonary embolism
D-dimer rises with fibrinolysis anywhere in the body, including after trauma, and is useful as a rule-out test for both deep vein thrombosis and pulmonary embolism. It is not limited to one disease.
It reflects fibrinolysis from many causes

Correct. D-dimer elevation implies increased fibrinolysis, but it is sensitive and not specific. Bruising, surgery, cancer and many other conditions raise it, so a positive result needs imaging while a negative one helps rule out a clot.
It rises only with thigh clots
D-dimer does not localize a clot to the thigh or anywhere else. It reflects fibrinolysis from many causes, so ultrasound is needed to find and locate any thrombus.
It is specific but not sensitive
This reverses the facts: D-dimer is sensitive but not specific. Its sensitivity is why a negative result helps rule out a clot, and its poor specificity is why a positive one needs imaging.

Thrombolysis is used for large proximal deep vein thrombosis or a stable pulmonary embolism. A short superficial clot is treated with compresses, compression, elevation and an anti-inflammatory drug.

B.q: A 41-year-old woman with dilated cardiomyopathy also has enlarged hilar lymph nodes and skin nodules, and an infiltrative process such as sarcoidosis is suspected. Coronary angiography showed no disease. Which imaging test best identifies an inflammatory or infiltrative cause?
opts: Cardiac magnetic resonance imaging with gadolinium
Correct. Cardiac magnetic resonance imaging with gadolinium contrast helps identify inflammatory, ischemic or infiltrative processes such as sarcoidosis or hemochromatosis in dilated cardiomyopathy.
A repeat resting electrocardiogram in six months
Repeating the electrocardiogram adds rhythm and conduction information only. Tissue characterization for sarcoidosis needs cardiac magnetic resonance imaging with gadolinium.

Ambulatory rhythm monitoring for forty-eight hours
Ambulatory monitoring assesses arrhythmia and sudden death risk, most notably in hypertrophic cardiomyopathy. It cannot show infiltration of the heart muscle.

B.q: A 27-year-old woman recovering well from her first episode of acute viral pericarditis asks how likely it is to come back. Which estimate is most accurate?
opts: Recurrence is much more common than 1%; about 15 to 30% of patients have another episode.
Correct. Recurrent pericarditis affects about 15 to 30% of patients after acute pericarditis, which is why completing the full course and recognizing symptoms early matter.
Sixty percent overstates the risk. About 15 to 30% of patients have a recurrence.
Recurrence is common but far from universal: it follows about 15 to 30% of acute episodes, so most patients never have a second episode.

B.q: A 79-year-old man has a preoperative electrocardiogram before cataract surgery. He feels well. His heart rate is 70, every P wave is followed by a narrow QRS complex, and the PR interval is constant at 0.26 seconds on every beat. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Mobitz type I (Wenckebach) block lengthens the PR from beat to beat until a QRS is dropped. Here the PR is constant and every beat conducts.
Mobitz type II keeps a constant PR but drops QRS complexes at random. Here every P wave is followed by a QRS, so nothing is dropped.

Correct. A constant PR interval longer than 0.20 seconds with every P wave conducted to a narrow QRS is first-degree atrioventricular block, most often from age-related degeneration of the conduction system.
Complete block dissociates P waves from QRS complexes at two different rates. Here each P wave leads its own QRS at a fixed interval.

B.q: Uremic pericarditis is typically associated with a blood urea nitrogen above which level?
opts: Ten mg/dL is a normal blood urea nitrogen. The uremic cause of pericarditis is associated with levels above 60 mg/dL.
A blood urea nitrogen of 20 mg/dL is near the upper limit of normal and would not explain pericarditis. Uremic pericarditis is tied to levels above 60 mg/dL.
Correct. Uremic pericarditis is linked to a blood urea nitrogen above 60 mg/dL; there will be laboratory evidence and a history of kidney disease, and it is treated with dialysis.
Uremic pericarditis does not wait for 200 mg/dL. It is associated with a blood urea nitrogen above 60 mg/dL.

B.q: A 52-year-old woman with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease has a rhythm strip in which a normal beat is followed by an early beat with an abnormal P wave and a narrow QRS, repeating so that every other beat is early (bigeminy). Which is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Flutter shows continuous sawtooth waves at 250 or more, not alternating normal and early beats.
Premature ventricular beats are early, wide and bizarre with no P wave; hers have abnormal P waves and narrow QRS complexes.
ruled out by a stated finding
A junctional rhythm is a steady slow rhythm at 40 to 60 with inverted or hidden P waves, not alternating early beats.
Correct. Early beats with an abnormal P wave and narrow QRS are premature atrial contractions (common in chronic lung disease), and an ectopic beat every other beat is bigeminy.

B.q: A 70-year-old man who had a large anterior myocardial infarction three weeks ago develops sudden pain and coldness of his right leg with absent foot pulses. Which cardiac finding is the most likely embolic source?
opts: Fluid around the heart does not form emboli. The cardiac sources named for limb emboli are atrial fibrillation and left ventricular thrombus after infarction.
A septal scar is not a recognized embolic source here. Following myocardial infarction, a left ventricular thrombus can dislodge and occlude a smaller distal artery.

Correct. Thromboemboli are the most common emboli, and the heart is the source in 80 to 90% of cases; a left ventricular thrombus after myocardial infarction is a named example, as is atrial fibrillation.
Valve calcification is not the named cardiac source. After a myocardial infarction, a left ventricular thrombus is the classic origin of an embolus to the leg.

B.q: A 21-year-old man has mild breathlessness and fatigue two weeks after a viral upper respiratory infection. Troponin is mildly raised, echocardiogram shows mildly reduced function, and he is hemodynamically stable. Which is the mainstay of his treatment?
opts: Most patients with mild symptoms recover completely, so transplant listing has no place here. Supportive care is the mainstay of treatment.

Correct. Treatment of myocarditis is directed toward the clinical scenario, and supportive care is the mainstay, with vasodilators, angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitors, diuretics, antiarrhythmics or anticoagulation as needed.
Biopsy is reserved for acute deterioration of unknown origin not responding to treatment. A stable patient with mild symptoms is managed with supportive care.
Alcohol septal ablation treats outflow obstruction in hypertrophic cardiomyopathy. Myocarditis is treated with supportive care directed at the clinical scenario.

B.io: Identify medical care strategies for infective endocarditis for the following populations. 8. infant 9. child 10. adolescent 11. adult 12. elderly
B.q: How are antibiotics for pediatric infective endocarditis given?
opts: Antibiotics are the backbone of treatment and start without waiting for surgery, given intravenously and weight-based.
Pediatric treatment is intravenous, not intramuscular, and weight-based rather than fixed-dose.
Correct. Pediatric therapy is prolonged, bactericidal, parenteral (intravenous, not intramuscular), pathogen-directed and weight-based, with the same empiric therapy as adults.
Oral, one-week therapy cannot sterilize a vegetation. Children get prolonged, intravenous, weight-based therapy.

B.q: A 71-year-old woman with suspected endocarditis has a urinalysis sent as part of her workup. Which urinalysis result is most consistent with endocarditis?
opts: Correct. Urinalysis in endocarditis can show hematuria, proteinuria and pyuria, reflecting renal involvement such as glomerulonephritis or emboli.
Nitrites without cells is not the pattern; hematuria, proteinuria and pyuria are.
Glucose and ketones point to diabetes, not endocarditis, whose urinalysis shows hematuria, proteinuria and pyuria.
Urine bilirubin and urobilinogen point to liver or hemolytic disease, not endocarditis.

B.q: A 65-year-old woman has new atrial fibrillation at 146 with palpitations. She is alert, her blood pressure is 132/84, and she has no chest pain or breathlessness. Which is the most appropriate initial treatment?
opts: Synchronized cardioversion is for the hemodynamically unstable patient; she is alert with a normal blood pressure.
Correct. A hemodynamically stable patient in atrial fibrillation with rapid ventricular response gets intravenous rate control; rate control is the first goal.
Atropine speeds the heart and is for unstable bradycardia; it would worsen rapid ventricular response.
Mapping and ablation is a later, elective rhythm option, not the first treatment of rapid ventricular response.

B.q: A 15-year-old girl nearly fainted twice while standing in the lunch line; both times she felt better once she lay down. She plays competitive soccer. A systolic murmur is heard at the left sternal border that becomes louder with the Valsalva maneuver. Which is the most appropriate next step?
opts: Recheck the murmur in a year
Delaying a year ignores a high-risk warning sign. Presyncope in suspected hypertrophic cardiomyopathy calls for an urgent work-up starting with echocardiography.
Clear her to play next week
Sudden death in hypertrophic cardiomyopathy is highest in adolescents and related to extreme exertion. She must not return to sport before an urgent evaluation.

Correct. Presyncope on standing relieved by lying down, like syncope, identifies patients with hypertrophic cardiomyopathy at high risk of sudden death, so the work-up is urgent, and echocardiography is the typical test of choice.
Presyncope with a murmur that grows louder with the Valsalva maneuver marks high sudden death risk in hypertrophic cardiomyopathy. Reassurance would delay an urgent work-up.

B.q: A 61-year-old man has a stable, regular narrow complex tachycardia at 150 in which P waves cannot be clearly seen. Adenosine is given. Besides possibly ending the rhythm, what can it reveal?
opts: A bundle branch block widens the QRS; adenosine slows the ventricular rate to show the hidden atrial activity.
Correct. Adenosine may convert a supraventricular tachycardia to normal sinus rhythm, or at least slow the rate so you can see whether P waves are there.
Adenosine is not given to uncover infarction; slowing the ventricular rate shows whether there are hidden P waves.
QT prolongation is a risk for torsades de pointes; adenosine's diagnostic use in a narrow tachycardia is revealing P waves.

B.q: A 70-year-old man has 3 weeks of low-grade fever and malaise that began a week after a dental extraction. A new murmur of mitral regurgitation is heard. Three sets of blood cultures are drawn. Which organism are they most likely to grow?
opts: Enterococci come from the genitourinary tract, not the mouth; an oral source after dental work brings viridans streptococci.
Staphylococcus aureus is a skin organism that causes acute, toxic disease; a smoldering course after dental work points to viridans streptococci.
Candida causes fungal endocarditis in the immunocompromised and in patients with central lines, not subacute disease after a tooth extraction.
Correct. The oral cavity is the source of viridans streptococci, the classic cause of subacute endocarditis after dental procedures and the organism dental prophylaxis targets.

B.q: A 57-year-old woman with dilated cardiomyopathy returns with recurring ankle edema and increasing abdominal girth. She admits to eating canned soups and fast food most days. Which dietary counseling point is most appropriate?
opts: Restrict sodium to under two grams a day
Correct. Patient education for dilated cardiomyopathy includes sodium restriction to less than two grams a day, along with the medication regimen, follow-up and removing any offending source.
No diet change is needed with drugs
Medication does not replace dietary control. Sodium restriction below two grams a day sits alongside the drug regimen in dilated cardiomyopathy education.
Raise salt intake to protect pressure
Extra salt worsens sodium and water retention and the edema she already has. Education for dilated cardiomyopathy is sodium restriction below two grams a day.
Drink extra fluids with every meal
Extra fluid adds to the congestion behind her edema. The dietary point taught for dilated cardiomyopathy is restricting sodium to under two grams a day.

B.q: What is the prognosis of viridans streptococcal infective endocarditis?
opts: Staphylococcus aureus is the most lethal organism; viridans streptococci carry a relatively good prognosis if treated before complications.
Prompt treatment is what makes the outlook relatively good: viridans streptococcal endocarditis does well if antibiotics start before complications.
A 30-40% valve-replacement rate is described for enterococcal endocarditis, not viridans streptococci.
Correct. Viridans streptococcal endocarditis has a relatively good prognosis if antibiotic treatment is started before complications occur.

B.q: A 55-year-old woman taking a loop diuretic for heart failure has new palpitations felt in her neck. Telemetry shows frequent premature ventricular contractions. Which laboratory values should be checked first?
opts: Glucose and lactate are not the named triggers. Low potassium and low magnesium are.
These look for infarction and pancreatitis. Frequent premature beats on a diuretic call for potassium and magnesium.
Correct. Electrolyte imbalances, especially hypokalemia and hypomagnesemia (with hypercalcemia), are main causes of premature ventricular contractions, and a loop diuretic can lower both.
Thyroid and adrenal tests are not the first step. Premature ventricular contractions call for potassium and magnesium levels.

B.q: What does the transthoracic echocardiogram show in Takotsubo (stress) cardiomyopathy?
opts: Septal wall of 1.5 cm or more
Wall thickness of 1.5 cm or more confirms hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, not stress cardiomyopathy.
Enlarged atria with near-normal, stiff ventricles fit restrictive cardiomyopathy, not stress cardiomyopathy.
Four-chamber dilation with thin walls is dilated cardiomyopathy. Stress cardiomyopathy gives regional mid and apical hypokinesis.
Correct. The transthoracic echocardiogram shows wall-motion abnormality, hypokinesis or akinesis of the midsegment and apical segment of the left ventricle.

B.q: A 50-year-old man with acute pericarditis says the pain keeps him awake because it is worse when he lies down. Which advice is most appropriate?
opts: Sleep prone to splint the chest
Prone sleeping is not recommended. Elevating the head of the bed eases positional pericardial pain.
Sleep flat to rest the heart
Lying flat is exactly what worsens his pain. The head of the bed should be raised.
Keep the head of the bed elevated
Correct. Pericardial pain is worse supine and better leaning forward, so keeping the head of the bed elevated is advised, along with completing the full treatment course.
Take an extra dose at bedtime
Extra bedtime medication does not address positional pain; elevating the head of the bed eases it.

B.q: Idarucizumab is the reversal agent for which anticoagulant?
opts: Correct. Idarucizumab reverses dabigatran in life-threatening or intracranial hemorrhage; each reversal agent is specific to its anticoagulant.
Apixaban is reversed by andexanet alfa, as is rivaroxaban. Idarucizumab reverses dabigatran, not the factor Xa inhibitors.
Warfarin is reversed with prothrombin complex concentrate, plasma or vitamin K. Idarucizumab reverses dabigatran.
Heparin is reversed by protamine sulfate, not idarucizumab. Idarucizumab reverses the direct thrombin inhibitor dabigatran.

B.q: A 76-year-old man has had symmetric pitting swelling of both ankles for three weeks. He started amlodipine for hypertension one month ago. There is no warmth, redness, tenderness or skin discoloration, and he has no history of heart, kidney or liver disease. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Chronic venous insufficiency produces brownish pigmentation, dermatitis and eventually ulceration after years of venous hypertension. Three weeks of bland swelling after a new drug does not fit.
Deep vein thrombosis is usually unilateral and brings pain, warmth and erythema. Symmetric painless swelling that began after a new drug without inflammation fits medication-induced edema.
Correct. Swelling that is often bilateral, without signs of inflammation, is a common adverse effect of some drugs, including dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers such as amlodipine.
Lymphedema is chronic swelling, usually unilateral, often after pelvic surgery, malignancy or radiation. This bilateral swelling began soon after starting a calcium channel blocker.

B.q: A 66-year-old man with hypertension has sudden, severe, ripping chest pain. His electrocardiogram is normal. Which is the most appropriate next step?
opts: The ankle-brachial index grades leg arterial disease. Suspected dissection is imaged with computed tomography of the chest and abdomen.
A plain film cannot show an intimal tear or false lumen. Computed tomography of the chest and abdomen delineates the extent.
Correct. The electrocardiogram may be normal in aortic dissection, so a normal tracing does not exclude it; computed tomography of the chest and abdomen delineates the extent of the dissection.
Reassure him; the tracing is normal
A normal electrocardiogram is common in aortic dissection and does not rule it out. Sudden tearing pain needs computed tomography of the chest and abdomen.

B.q: A 52-year-old man with a pacemaker implanted two weeks ago has three days of swelling and aching of the left arm. The pacemaker lead has injured the wall of the subclavian vein. Which component of the Virchow triad does this injury represent?
opts: Correct. Damage to the vessel lining from an indwelling device is endothelial trauma, one leg of the Virchow triad. Pacemakers, implanted defibrillators and central venous catheters are the most common causes of upper-extremity deep vein thrombosis.
A hypercoagulable state is a clotting tendency from inherited disorders, cancer, estrogen or pregnancy. Mechanical injury to the vein wall from a lead is endothelial trauma instead.
Impaired lymphatic drainage causes lymphedema and is not part of the Virchow triad. Injury to the subclavian vein wall is endothelial trauma, the third triad component.
Venous stasis arises from immobilization, heart failure or venous insufficiency. A lead scraping the vein wall is physical injury to the lining, which is the endothelial trauma component.

B.q: A 72-year-old man has months of progressive breathlessness, abdominal swelling and bilateral pedal edema. He prefers to sit upright. Jugular venous pressure is raised and he has a Kussmaul sign (jugular venous pressure rises with inspiration), hepatomegaly and ascites. His electrocardiogram shows low voltage (small complexes) in all leads, and echocardiogram shows normal-sized ventricles, marked biatrial enlargement and a preserved ejection fraction. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy shows asymmetric septal thickening with an outflow murmur and prominent Q waves rather than low voltage. Right-sided congestion with big atria fits restrictive disease.

Correct. Stiff ventricles with a near-normal cavity, preserved ejection fraction and big atria, presenting late with right-sided failure, are restrictive cardiomyopathy; low voltage points to amyloidosis, the most common cause in the United States.
Stress cardiomyopathy is a sudden, transient apical weakness after a stressor. Months of right-sided congestion with stiff ventricles and big atria is restrictive disease.
Dilated cardiomyopathy shows dilated, thin-walled ventricles with a reduced ejection fraction. Normal-sized ventricles with a preserved fraction and big atria are restrictive.

B.q: What makes up atheroemboli?
opts: Marrow fat is not the material described. Atheroemboli are fibrin, platelets and cholesterol debris from proximal plaques.
Clot formed in the left atrium
Atrial clot gives thromboemboli, the usual cause of acute limb ischemia. Atheroemboli are fibrin, platelets and cholesterol debris.
Correct. Atheroembolism is multiple small deposits of fibrin, platelets and cholesterol debris embolizing from proximal atherosclerotic lesions.
Air is not part of atheroembolism. The emboli are fibrin, platelets and cholesterol debris from plaques.

B.q: A 64-year-old woman has two weeks of exertional breathlessness and chest pressure. Her electrocardiogram shows a left bundle branch block; a tracing from last year was normal. Which is the most appropriate next step?
opts: Some new right bundle branch blocks occur without heart disease, but a new left bundle branch block is a sign of pathology that needs evaluation.
Correct. A new left bundle branch block should always be considered a sign of pathology, so it is worked up for the underlying cardiac disease or injury rather than dismissed.
Left bundle branch block is usually not paced unless it is symptomatic with reduced ejection fraction, which calls for a biventricular device after evaluation.
Cardioversion terminates tachycardias; a conduction block with a normal rate is not shocked. The new block needs a workup.

B.q: Besides shocking, what can newer implantable cardioverter defibrillators also do?
opts: Ablation is done with a catheter, not by the implanted device. Newer defibrillators can also pace.
The device does not infuse drugs. Newer implantable defibrillators can also act as pacemakers.
Clot dissolution needs a thrombolytic or a catheter procedure. Newer defibrillators add pacing to their shocking function.
Correct. Newer implantable defibrillators can also act as pacemakers, in addition to sensing fatal arrhythmias and delivering a shock.

B.q: A 70-year-old man with chronic kidney disease has native valve endocarditis from penicillin-susceptible viridans streptococci. The team is choosing his antibiotic plan. Which choice should be avoided?
opts: Ceftriaxone is a standard directed agent for viridans streptococci and does not depend on gentamicin.

Correct. The 2-week regimen with gentamicin is reserved for uncomplicated endocarditis with a rapid response and no chronic kidney disease; gentamicin is nephrotoxic, so he needs a standard course without it.
Penicillin G for the full course
Penicillin G is a standard directed agent for viridans streptococci and is appropriate for him.
Close monitoring of labs and renal function is part of endocarditis management, especially with kidney disease.

B.q: A 66-year-old woman with a 4.8 cm abdominal aortic aneurysm has a history of severe reaction to contrast dye. She is stable, and the extent of the aneurysm must be defined. Which imaging is most appropriate?
opts: Computed tomography angiography relies on contrast dye, which her allergy precludes. Magnetic resonance imaging gives comparable detail without dye.
A plain film shows only a calcified outline, and misses a quarter of aneurysms. It cannot define extent; magnetic resonance imaging can, without dye.
Conventional angiography needs contrast injection into the artery. For a stable patient with dye allergy, magnetic resonance imaging is the alternative.
Correct. Magnetic resonance imaging is comparable to computed tomography without exposure to dye or ionizing radiation, which makes it useful in stable patients with a dye allergy.

B.q: When right bundle branch block causes symptoms, what do they usually point to?
opts: Electrolyte disturbances drive premature ventricular contractions. Symptomatic right bundle branch block points to severe underlying heart disease.
A new right bundle branch block can be benign when silent, but symptoms usually point to severe underlying heart disease.
An accessory pathway causes pre-excitation, not bundle branch block symptoms. Symptoms usually point to severe underlying heart disease.
Correct. Right bundle branch block is usually asymptomatic; patients who develop symptoms usually have severe underlying cardiac disease, with heart failure-like symptoms.

B.q: A 61-year-old man underwent cardiac catheterization through the right femoral artery and vein ten days ago. He now has a continuous machine-like murmur over the puncture site with a palpable thrill (a vibration felt over the skin), and his right leg is swollen with prominent superficial veins. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Correct. Femoral puncture for percutaneous access can connect the artery and vein, and the bruit and thrill with venous congestion of the leg follow. Lower extremity fistulas are most commonly iatrogenic from groin access.
Deep vein thrombosis of the leg
Deep vein thrombosis gives swelling, pain and warmth but no bruit or thrill. A murmur over the puncture site indicates blood flowing between artery and vein.
A pseudoaneurysm is a pulsatile mass from arterial leakage contained by tissue. A continuous murmur with a thrill and venous congestion of the leg points to an abnormal artery to vein connection.
Superficial thrombophlebitis produces a tender palpable cord with redness along a vein. It does not create a continuous murmur and thrill over a femoral puncture.

opts: Enterococci cause about 4% of device endocarditis, far behind coagulase-negative staphylococci.
Streptococci cause only about 2% of device endocarditis; skin staphylococci dominate.

The HACEK (Haemophilus, Aggregatibacter, Cardiobacterium, Eikenella, Kingella) organisms come from the upper respiratory tract and are not a leading device organism; coagulase-negative staphylococci lead at about 41%.

Correct. Device endocarditis is caused mostly by coagulase-negative staphylococci (about 41%) and Staphylococcus aureus (about 36%), and it can appear within weeks of implantation or a generator change.

Procainamide is for atrial fibrillation with Wolff-Parkinson-White, not nodal reentry.

B.q: A 58-year-old man received chest radiation for lymphoma 20 years ago. He has 8 months of exertional dyspnea, fatigue, leg edema and ascites. His jugular venous pressure is elevated and shows the Kussmaul sign (it rises on inspiration instead of falling), and a pericardial knock (an early diastolic sound, slightly earlier than a third heart sound) is heard. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Correct. Fluid overload with low output, an elevated jugular venous pressure with the Kussmaul sign and a pericardial knock after prior radiation are the picture of constrictive pericarditis, scarring that limits filling.
Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy causes outflow obstruction and a systolic murmur, not a knock with a Kussmaul sign and ascites.
Acute pericarditis presents with sharp pleuritic, positional pain and a friction rub, not months of edema, ascites and a Kussmaul sign.
Endocarditis presents with fever, a new murmur and embolic signs, not the fluid overload and Kussmaul sign of constriction.

B.q: A 74-year-old woman has months of fatigue and two near-faints. Repeated electrocardiograms show sinus bradycardia at 42, and her symptoms match the slow rate. She takes no rate-slowing drugs and her thyroid tests are normal. Which treatment is indicated?
opts: Ablation destroys tissue causing a tachycardia; it cannot speed a slow sinus node.
Correct. Chronic, symptomatic sinus bradycardia with no reversible cause, as here in an older adult, is managed with a permanent pacemaker.
Cardioversion resets fast rhythms; chronic symptomatic sinus bradycardia needs a permanent pacemaker.
Atropine is a short-acting rescue for acute, unstable bradycardia, not long-term therapy for chronic symptomatic disease.

Drug therapy alone is for stable monomorphic ventricular tachycardia. Polymorphic ventricular tachycardia needs defibrillation.
Correct. Polymorphic ventricular tachycardia is never truly stable, only a short-lived transitional state, so it is defibrillated even when the patient has a pulse and looks well.
Synchronized cardioversion needs a consistent QRS; it suits unstable monomorphic rhythm. Polymorphic ventricular tachycardia is defibrillated.

B.q: A 72-year-old woman has ischemic rest pain and a nonhealing toe ulcer, with an ankle-brachial index of 0.3. Angiography shows a long femoral-popliteal occlusion. Which treatment is principally used for her degree of disease?
opts: Intravenous heparin is for acute peripheral arterial occlusion. Chronic critical limb ischemia with a long occlusion is principally treated with a bypass graft.
Pentoxifylline is a xanthine derivative given for claudication symptoms. It cannot rescue a limb with rest pain and an ulcer; bypass grafting is the principal treatment.
Exercise therapy improves walking distance in claudication. Rest pain with tissue loss is critical limb ischemia, which is principally treated with a bypass graft.
Correct. A bypass graft, using a saphenous vein or synthetic graft around the diseased segment, is principally used to treat severe critical leg ischemia and is highly effective.

B.q: A 60-year-old man with carotid artery disease on duplex smokes a pack a day and asks whether quitting still matters now that he takes aspirin. Which counseling point is accurate?
opts: Correct. Smoking cessation is part of medical management of carotid disease because smoking nearly doubles the risk of stroke; it sits alongside antiplatelet therapy, comorbidity control, diet, exercise and weight reduction.
Smoking harms only the leg arteries
Smoking drives atherosclerosis throughout the body and nearly doubles stroke risk. Cessation is central to managing carotid disease.
Smoking cessation is part of medical management for every patient with carotid disease, surgical or not, because smoking nearly doubles stroke risk.
Antiplatelet therapy does not neutralize tobacco. Smoking nearly doubles stroke risk, so cessation remains a core part of carotid disease management.

opts: She is stable, and a polymorphic rhythm cannot be synchronized. Recurrent runs get a magnesium infusion.
Correct. Torsades in a conscious patient is broken with intravenous magnesium and then treated with more magnesium as an infusion: magnesium, and more magnesium.
Procainamide prolongs the QT and is avoided in torsades. A magnesium infusion follows the first push.
Amiodarone prolongs the QT and is avoided in torsades. Recurrent runs are treated with a magnesium infusion.

B.q: A 38-year-old man who injects drugs has finished a course of intravenous antibiotics for tricuspid valve endocarditis and is preparing for discharge. He says he wants help to stay safe. Which consultation should be arranged?
opts: Renal function is monitored during antibiotics, but harm reduction for injection drug use is addiction medicine's role.
Ophthalmology is not the consult for his drug use. Addiction medicine provides harm reduction.
Correct. Addiction medicine is consulted for harm reduction in people who inject drugs, part of the multidisciplinary care with infectious disease and cardiothoracic surgery.
Dermatology has no listed role; harm reduction for injection drug use comes from addiction medicine.

B.q: A 40-year-old woman with right lower lobe pneumonia has sharp chest pain. A rubbing sound is heard over the lower chest that is present only while she breathes in and vanishes when she holds her breath. Which is the most likely source of the sound?
opts: Valve murmurs do not disappear with breath-holding and are not rubs. This is a pleural rub.
A pericardial rub continues, and gets louder, when the breath is held, because only the heart is moving. This sound stopped with breath-holding.
ruled out by a stated finding
Correct. A pleural rub is tied to respiration, heard in the inspiratory phase, and disappears with breath-holding; a pericardial rub persists, and even intensifies, while the breath is held.
Chest wall pain is reproducible on palpation and makes no rubbing sound. A rub that stops with breath-holding is pleural.

B.q: How does older age affect surgical intervention for pericardial disease?
opts: Correct. Older adults have higher morbidity and mortality with surgical interventions, including pericardiocentesis and pericardiectomy, and often need rehabilitation afterward.
Lower risk than in younger adults
Older adults carry higher, not lower, surgical risk for pericardial procedures, with more morbidity and mortality.
Age does change the risk: older adults have higher morbidity and mortality with surgical interventions.
Surgery is not ruled out by age; it carries higher morbidity and mortality, which is weighed in the decision.

Which is the most appropriate next step?
opts: Synchronized cardioversion treats unstable tachycardias with a pulse. A slow rate from a failing conduction system needs pacing.
Correct. When medications are not used or do not work in unstable Mobitz type II block, the emergent measure is transcutaneous pacing, which bridges her to a permanent pacemaker.
Defibrillation is for ventricular fibrillation or pulseless ventricular tachycardia. She has a pulse and a slow, blocked rhythm.
Observation is unsafe with hypotension and confusion. Unstable Mobitz type II block is paced transcutaneously.

C.q: Adverse ventricular remodeling in dilated cardiomyopathy gives the heart which shape?
opts: A bulging, thick septum is the classic pattern of hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, not the globular remodeling that dilated cardiomyopathy produces.
A narrow tubular heart is not the remodeling pattern. Dilated cardiomyopathy produces the opposite: a globular, round heart with enlarged chambers.
Correct. Adverse ventricular remodeling leads to a globular (globe or round) shaped heart, with an increase in total cardiac mass and dilated chambers.
Normal ventricles with large atria belong to restrictive cardiomyopathy, where stiff ventricles make both atria enlarge from impaired filling.

C.q: A 52-year-old man starts outpatient treatment for deep vein thrombosis with low molecular weight heparin injections overlapped with warfarin. The injections continue for at least five days and until his international normalized ratio is above which value?
opts: An international normalized ratio just above 1 is barely different from normal, so warfarin has not yet taken effect. The overlap continues until the value is above 2.

Correct. Parenteral therapy overlaps with warfarin for at least five days and until the international normalized ratio is above 2, when warfarin has reached its therapeutic effect and the heparin can stop.
The overlap ends once the international normalized ratio is above 2, the therapeutic threshold for this indication. Waiting for a value above 3 would prolong the injections without benefit.
An international normalized ratio above 4 is over-anticoagulated and raises the bleeding risk. The heparin overlap stops once warfarin is therapeutic, at a value above 2.

C.q: A 64-year-old woman with mitral valve endocarditis has 2 days of worsening breathlessness and orthopnea (breathlessness when lying flat). A new, loud regurgitant murmur is heard and crackles fill both lung bases. Which mechanism explains her heart failure?
opts: Correct. Congestive heart failure in infective endocarditis is due to valvular dysfunction, here from leaflet damage or chordal rupture, and it is the most common indication for surgery.
Fever does not cause the heart failure described. Destroyed valve function, with a new regurgitant murmur, is the mechanism.
Pericardial constriction is a separate disease. Endocarditis causes heart failure through valvular dysfunction.
Intravenous antibiotics are not the mechanism given; the new regurgitant murmur points to valvular dysfunction.

C.q: A 62-year-old woman on chemotherapy for breast cancer comes to the emergency department with a calf 4 cm larger than the other, tenderness along the deep veins and no better explanation, so her Wells score is high. Her D-dimer, drawn at triage, is negative. Which action should be avoided?
opts: Ultrasound is exactly what a high Wells score calls for, whatever the D-dimer shows. It is the appropriate next test, so ordering it is the right action, not one to avoid.
Ending the work-up at the D-dimer

Correct. With a high Wells score the D-dimer is skipped, or if it was drawn, a negative result does not end the evaluation: she still goes to venous duplex ultrasound. Stopping here risks missing a clot with high pretest probability.
Comparing the calves at a set point below the tibial tuberosity is how the Wells item for swelling over 3 cm is scored. It is a useful step, not an error.
Pointed questions about breathing are part of the evaluation, because the lower-extremity clot can send an embolus to the lungs. This is good practice rather than a mistake to avoid.

opts: Oral rate control is for the stable patient; hypotension and confusion call for synchronized cardioversion.
Vagal maneuvers are first line for stable supraventricular tachycardia; unstable flutter needs synchronized cardioversion.
Three weeks of anticoagulation precedes elective outpatient cardioversion; an unstable patient is cardioverted now.
Correct. Hemodynamically unstable atrial flutter (hypotension with confusion) is treated with synchronized cardioversion.

C.q: A 62-year-old woman receiving chemotherapy through a central venous catheter has two days of right arm swelling and aching. The catheter injuring the vein wall is the endothelial trauma component of the Virchow triad. Which is the best diagnostic test?
opts: D-dimer is nonspecific and is often elevated in cancer, so a positive result cannot confirm a clot and cannot replace imaging. Venous duplex ultrasound is the test that shows the thrombus.
The ankle-brachial index compares ankle and arm pressures to detect peripheral artery disease in the legs. It does not evaluate a swollen arm for a venous clot.
Contrast ascending venography was the gold standard but is invasive and has been replaced by venous duplex ultrasound. It is not the first test for a catheter-related arm clot.

Correct. Venous duplex ultrasound of the involved extremity is the diagnostic test for deep vein thrombosis, including arm clots from central venous catheters. It has replaced venography, the old invasive gold standard.
