C.q: A 34-year-old man who injects heroin has 4 days of fever to 39.6 °C (103.3 °F), rigors and a cough. A new holosystolic murmur is heard at the left lower sternal border, and he looks toxic. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Pneumonia would not explain a new holosystolic murmur in a person who injects drugs; fever, rigors, cough and that murmur point to tricuspid valve endocarditis.
Pericarditis brings positional chest pain and a friction rub, not a new holosystolic murmur with rigors in a person who injects drugs.

Correct. In people who inject drugs the tricuspid valve is the valve singled out (Staphylococcus aureus causes 80-90% of those infections); cough is linked to this group, and a holosystolic murmur at the left lower sternal border fits the tricuspid valve.
A mitral murmur is loudest at the apex, not the left lower sternal border, and in people who inject drugs the valve singled out is the tricuspid.

The electrocardiogram shows a regular narrow complex tachycardia with no visible P waves. Which is the most appropriate first step?
opts: Adenosine is the second step for stable supraventricular tachycardia, given if a vagal maneuver fails.
Correct. A stable, regular narrow complex tachycardia above 160 with hidden P waves is supraventricular tachycardia, and the first-line treatment when stable is a vagal maneuver, then adenosine.
Immediate synchronized cardioversion is for the hemodynamically unstable patient; she is alert with a normal blood pressure.
Procainamide is reserved for atrial fibrillation with Wolff-Parkinson-White; a stable narrow complex tachycardia starts with a vagal maneuver.

C.q: A 70-year-old woman being treated for an acute aortic dissection develops a new diastolic murmur and worsening breathlessness. Which complication explains these findings?
opts: Correct. Aortic dissection can cause aortic regurgitation through dilatation of the aortic root, producing a diastolic murmur and breathlessness.
A pseudoaneurysm follows arterial puncture and causes local swelling and pain. The new diastolic murmur here is aortic regurgitation from root dilatation.
Mitral stenosis is not a listed consequence of dissection. Root dilatation in dissection causes aortic regurgitation.
Carotid stenosis is an atherosclerotic narrowing that produces neurologic symptoms, not a diastolic murmur. Root dilatation causes aortic regurgitation.

C.q: A 71-year-old woman with restrictive cardiomyopathy and marked biatrial enlargement has had palpitations for a week, and the electrocardiogram now shows atrial fibrillation. Which treatment reduces her risk of embolism?
opts: Diuretics treat congestion and must be used cautiously in restrictive disease; they do nothing to prevent emboli. Anticoagulation prevents embolism from atrial thrombi.

Correct. Atrial fibrillation is common in restrictive cardiomyopathy because of atrial enlargement, it raises the risk of atrial thrombus, and anticoagulants may be needed to prevent embolism from atrial thrombi.
Inotropes do not prevent thromboembolism. With atrial fibrillation and big atria, anticoagulation is used to prevent embolism.
Myectomy removes obstructing septal muscle in hypertrophic cardiomyopathy. Embolism from atrial thrombi in restrictive disease is prevented with anticoagulation.

C.q: A 45-year-old man has a heart rate of 122 with a normal P wave before every narrow QRS. His temperature is 39.2°C and he has a productive cough and crackles at the right base. He is alert with a blood pressure of 126/78. Which is the best treatment for his heart rate?
opts: Correct. A sinus tachycardia from fever and infection is an appropriate response to a pathologic process, and appropriate sinus tachycardia is managed by treating the underlying cause.
Vagal maneuvers are first line for reentrant supraventricular tachycardia; a fever-driven sinus tachycardia settles when the infection is treated.
Adenosine stops reentrant supraventricular tachycardia through the atrioventricular node; it has no role in a sinus tachycardia from fever.
Cardioversion is for unstable reentrant or fibrillatory rhythms; this stable sinus tachycardia needs its cause treated.

Paroxysmal supraventricular tachycardia
C.q: A slow sinus rhythm that is causing hypotension and confusion is treated first with which drug?
opts: Digoxin is a listed drug cause of sinus bradycardia and sick sinus syndrome, so it would slow the heart further rather than rescue it.
Metoprolol is a beta blocker, and beta blockers are a listed cause of sinus bradycardia; giving one would worsen the problem.
Adenosine blocks the atrioventricular node to stop supraventricular tachycardia; in a slow, unstable rhythm it would deepen the bradycardia.
Correct. Acute, symptomatic, hemodynamically unstable bradycardia is treated first with atropine, then a temporary pacemaker if it fails; chronic symptomatic disease needs a permanent pacemaker.

C.q: What is the common site of a pseudoaneurysm?
opts: Bypass complications are listed separately. Pseudoaneurysm is typically femoral after cardiac catheterization.
The infrarenal aorta is the site of true abdominal aneurysms. Pseudoaneurysm typically affects the femoral artery after catheterization.
Endarterectomy's complications are stroke or nerve damage. Pseudoaneurysm typically follows femoral catheterization.
Correct. The common site is the femoral artery after cardiac catheterization, caused by laceration of the artery by the access needle.

C.q: A 22-year-old man has recovered from mild viral myocarditis and feels well at discharge. He asks whether he needs any long-term follow-up with a cardiologist. Which later complication does follow-up watch for?
opts: Restrictive cardiomyopathy follows infiltration, storage disease, sarcoidosis or radiation and chemotherapy. After myocarditis, the late risk is dilated cardiomyopathy.

Correct. Most patients with mild myocarditis recover completely, but one third subsequently develop dilated cardiomyopathy, and viral myocarditis accounts for about 20% of dilated cardiomyopathy cases.
Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy is mostly inherited through sarcomere gene mutations and is not a consequence of myocarditis. One third of patients later develop dilated cardiomyopathy.
Takotsubo cardiomyopathy is a transient response to emotional or physical stress, mostly in postmenopausal women. Myocarditis leads on to dilated cardiomyopathy in one third.

C.q: A 66-year-old woman with ovarian cancer has had three drainages for a recurrent pericardial effusion, and the latest echocardiogram shows a loculated collection behind the heart. Which procedure is most appropriate?
opts: Diuretics do not drain a malignant loculated effusion. A pericardial window does.
A posterior loculated collection cannot be reached percutaneously, and repeat taps fail with recurrence; a window is needed.
Thoracentesis drains the pleural space, not the pericardium. A pericardial window is the procedure.
Correct. A pericardiectomy or pericardial window is performed for recurrent effusions and for loculated effusions, especially posterior ones that cannot be approached percutaneously.

C.q: A 29-year-old woman has superficial thrombophlebitis of the forearm after an intravenous catheter and asks whether the clot can travel to her lungs. Which statement about her outlook is accurate?
opts: Pulmonary embolism is the usual outcome
Pulmonary embolism is the feared complication of deep vein thrombosis. Superficial thrombophlebitis rarely embolizes, so this outcome is the exception rather than the rule.

Correct. Superficial phlebitis and thrombophlebitis rarely cause serious complications and rarely embolize, which distinguishes them from deep vein thrombosis, where pulmonary embolism is the major complication.
Chronic venous insufficiency follows in most
Chronic venous insufficiency is a late result of deep vein thrombosis that scars the valves. It is not the expected outcome of an uncomplicated superficial thrombophlebitis.
Fatal embolism is likely without treatment
Even untreated deep vein thrombosis carries a small rate of fatal embolism. A superficial clot rarely embolizes at all, so a fatal event is not expected.

C.q: A 68-year-old woman has atrial fibrillation found at a routine visit. Her heart rate is 84, she has no symptoms of instability, and her blood pressure is 128/76. Which is the most appropriate rate management?
opts: Correct. A hemodynamically stable patient in atrial fibrillation without rapid ventricular response is managed with rate control by mouth, with anticoagulation guided by stroke risk.
Intravenous rate control is for rapid ventricular response; her rate of 84 is already controlled.
Atropine speeds the heart and is used for unstable bradycardia; it has no role in rate-controlled atrial fibrillation.
Cardioversion is for instability or elective rhythm control after anticoagulation; she is stable.

C.q: A 30-year-old cyclist with no symptoms has a rhythm in which the PR interval lengthens beat by beat until a QRS complex is dropped, after which the cycle starts again. Echocardiogram is normal. Which is the most appropriate management?
opts: Transcutaneous pacing is an emergency bridge for unstable high-grade block. Stable, silent Mobitz type I needs no treatment.
Ablation destroys conduction tissue and is itself a named cause of Mobitz type I. A silent block needs no treatment.
A pacemaker is for symptomatic Mobitz type I, or for Mobitz type II even without symptoms. A symptom-free cyclist needs no treatment.
Correct. Asymptomatic Mobitz type I block needs no treatment; a permanent pacemaker is considered only for debilitating symptoms or heart failure symptoms.

C.q: A 78-year-old man with recurrent urinary tract infections has aortic valve endocarditis, and his blood cultures grow Enterococcus faecalis. Which regimen is most appropriate?
opts: Nafcillin plus rifampin belongs to staphylococcal prosthetic valve therapy, not enterococcal disease.
Cefazolin is a methicillin-susceptible staphylococcal option, not an enterococcal regimen.
A single oral amoxicillin dose is dental prophylaxis, not treatment of established endocarditis.
Correct. Enterococcal endocarditis is treated with ampicillin (or penicillin G) plus gentamicin, ampicillin plus ceftriaxone, or vancomycin plus gentamicin.

opts: Hyperthyroidism speeds the sinus node; it does not produce a slow junctional rhythm.
Missing doses lowers the digoxin effect rather than slowing the heart further; nausea and fatigue with a slow junctional rhythm point to digoxin toxicity, a listed cause.
An accessory pathway causes pre-excitation and fast reentry, not a slow junctional rhythm.
Correct. A slow regular narrow rhythm with inverted P waves after the QRS is a junctional rhythm, and digoxin toxicity is a listed cause.

C.q: A 35-year-old woman has 3 days of sharp substernal chest pain that improves when she sits forward. Her vital signs are normal, and no rub is heard on careful auscultation. Which additional finding would complete the clinical diagnosis of acute pericarditis?
opts: Correct. The diagnosis needs two of four criteria: sharp substernal chest pain, a friction rub, suggestive electrocardiogram changes (widespread ST elevation) and a new or worsening effusion. Her pain plus the electrocardiogram would make two.
The natriuretic peptide belongs to the constriction workup and is not a pericarditis criterion. Widespread ST elevation would complete the diagnosis.
A troponin above the reference range
Troponin is not a diagnostic criterion; an elevated value would suggest myocardial involvement (myopericarditis) and higher risk.
Calcification points to long-standing constriction, not acute pericarditis, and is not one of the four criteria.

C.q: Which Virchow triad component can be inherited or acquired?
opts: Endothelial trauma is acquired, from surgery, injury, burns or injected drug use. The hypercoagulable state is the component with inherited forms too.
Correct. A hypercoagulable state can be inherited (factor V Leiden, prothrombin gene mutation, protein C or S or antithrombin deficiency) or acquired (cancer, estrogen, pregnancy).
Only one component has inherited forms: the hypercoagulable state. Stasis and endothelial trauma are acquired.
Stasis is acquired, arising from immobilization, venous insufficiency or heart failure. The component with inherited and acquired forms is the hypercoagulable state.

C.q: A 45-year-old man who grew up in rural Bolivia has months of fatigue and exertional breathlessness. His heart rate is 38 and the electrocardiogram shows P waves completely dissociated from slow, wide QRS complexes. Which infection is a named cause of his conduction disease?
opts: Tuberculosis is not on the list of causes of complete block. Chagas disease, endemic in Latin America, is.
Lyme carditis is a named cause of block, but it follows a tick bite in endemic areas such as New England. His background points to Chagas disease.
Correct. Chagas disease is a named cause of complete heart block; it is a parasitic infection endemic in parts of Latin America such as rural Bolivia.
Malaria is not a named cause of complete block. A man from rural Bolivia with complete block suggests Chagas disease.

C.q: A 64-year-old man with claudication, diabetes and continued smoking is taking a statin. Which low-density lipoprotein target applies to him?
opts: Correct. Lipid-lowering therapy in peripheral artery disease targets a low-density lipoprotein below 100 mg/dL, and below 70 mg/dL for high-risk patients such as those with diabetes or continued smoking.
Below 100 mg/dL is the standard target in peripheral artery disease. Diabetes and continued smoking make him high risk, which lowers the target to below 70 mg/dL.
Below 130 mg/dL is looser than any target given for peripheral artery disease. The standard target is below 100 mg/dL and below 70 mg/dL for high risk.
Below 160 mg/dL would leave him far above goal. High-risk peripheral artery disease with diabetes or smoking targets a low-density lipoprotein below 70 mg/dL.

C.q: A 42-year-old woman has symptomatic varicose veins that did not improve with stockings. She prefers a nonsurgical procedure in which a solution is injected to scar and close the veins. Which procedure fits?
opts: Correct. Sclerotherapy is the injection of a sclerosing agent to fibrose and obliterate the veins, one of the interventions for varicose veins along with stripping and catheter-based ablation.
Bypass is successful in select patients with chronic venous insufficiency and is a major surgery. It does not close veins, which sclerotherapy does by injection.
Radiofrequency uses a catheter to treat reflux with heat, and nothing is injected. The injection of a solution to scar the vein is sclerotherapy.
Stripping is a surgical procedure that removes the vein rather than an injection that closes it. It is a surgical reflux treatment, not the injection she prefers.

C.q: A 69-year-old man has an asymptomatic abdominal aortic aneurysm measuring 4.7 cm on his latest ultrasound. Which referral is appropriate?
opts: Emergency surgery is for rupture, not a painless 4.7 cm aneurysm. The appropriate step is referral to a vascular team for observation and assessment.
Waiting for a repair threshold is too late for referral. From 4.5 cm a vascular team should observe and assess the aneurysm.
Correct. Aneurysms of 4.5 cm or larger warrant referral to a vascular team for observation and assessment, with urgent referral whenever the patient has aneurysmal pain, whatever the size.
Echocardiography does not assess an abdominal aneurysm. From 4.5 cm the referral is to a vascular team for observation and assessment.

C.q: A 62-year-old man with fever, a new murmur and positive blood cultures is stable. A transthoracic study is limited by his body habitus. Which imaging test best detects vegetations and defines the extent of disease?
opts: Repeating a limited transthoracic study adds little; the transesophageal study is the highly sensitive and specific one.
A chest radiograph cannot show valve vegetations; the transesophageal echocardiogram detects them and defines extent.
Correct. Transesophageal echocardiography is highly sensitive and specific, detects vegetations on the valve leaflets and defines the extent of disease.
Angiography images the coronary arteries, not valve vegetations; transesophageal echocardiography shows them.

Restrictive cardiomyopathy 3. Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy 4. Dilated cardiomyopathy 5. Stress cardiomyopathy 6. Myocarditis
C.q: A 16-year-old boy collapses briefly during a basketball game and recovers within a minute. Blood pressure and heart rate are normal. There is a crescendo-decrescendo systolic murmur at the left sternal border in the fourth intercostal space that does not radiate to the carotids; it grows louder when he stands and softer when he squats. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Restrictive cardiomyopathy is rare, presents late with right-sided congestion and big atria, and does not produce an outflow murmur that changes with standing and squatting.
Myocarditis follows a flulike illness with acute heart failure and elevated troponin. A posture-sensitive outflow murmur in an athlete points to hypertrophic cardiomyopathy.

Correct. Exertional syncope in an adolescent with an outflow murmur at the left sternal border that does not reach the carotids, louder with standing and softer with squatting, is obstructive hypertrophic cardiomyopathy.
Dilated cardiomyopathy gives heart failure symptoms with a displaced apical impulse, a third heart sound and regurgitant murmurs, not a dynamic outflow murmur that changes with posture.

C.q: Which patient with recurrent pericarditis is described as a candidate for anti-interleukin-1 therapy?
opts: Tamponade needs expedient pericardiocentesis, not a biologic. Anti-interleukin-1 therapy targets steroid-dependent or colchicine-resistant recurrence.
Correct. Recurrent or colchicine-resistant disease, or steroid-dependent disease, with an inflammatory phenotype makes anakinra or rilonacept the preferred option.
One with a first, mild episode
A first episode is treated with an anti-inflammatory plus colchicine for about 3 months. Anti-interleukin-1 therapy is for recurrent, resistant or steroid-dependent disease.
One with a normal C-reactive protein
A normal C-reactive protein argues against the inflammatory phenotype that anti-interleukin-1 therapy targets.

C.q: Which oral prophylaxis fits a patient with a penicillin allergy?
opts: Correct. Penicillin-allergic patients who can take oral medication receive azithromycin or clarithromycin, cephalexin (if no anaphylaxis, angioedema or urticaria) or doxycycline.
Amoxicillin is a penicillin, so it is avoided in penicillin allergy. Azithromycin or clarithromycin is an option.
ruled out by a stated finding
Ampicillin is a penicillin and is avoided in penicillin allergy; macrolides such as azithromycin are an option.
ruled out by a stated finding
Clindamycin is no longer recommended because of the risk of Clostridioides difficile infection.

C.q: How is polymorphic ventricular tachycardia treated, even when the patient has a pulse?
opts: Drug therapy alone is for stable monomorphic ventricular tachycardia. Polymorphic ventricular tachycardia is never stable and is defibrillated.
Watching is unsafe: polymorphic ventricular tachycardia is a transitional state that needs defibrillation.
Correct. Polymorphic ventricular tachycardia is never truly stable, only a short-lived transitional state, so it is defibrillated even if the patient looks well.
Synchronized shocks need a consistent QRS to time against. Polymorphic ventricular tachycardia is defibrillated, even with a pulse.

C.q: Adenosine slows a tachycardia and reveals atrial fibrillation with Wolff-Parkinson-White. Which drug is used?
opts: Magnesium is for torsades de pointes; pre-excited atrial fibrillation is treated with procainamide.
Atropine speeds the heart and treats unstable bradycardia; it would worsen a pre-excited tachycardia, which needs procainamide.
More adenosine blocks only the normal atrioventricular node and leaves the accessory pathway to carry the fibrillation; procainamide is used.

Correct. When slowing from adenosine reveals atrial fibrillation with Wolff-Parkinson-White, intravenous procainamide is used and adenosine is not repeated; adenosine and the other nodal blockers leave the accessory pathway unopposed.

C.q: A 66-year-old woman with aortic valve endocarditis has a transesophageal echocardiogram that shows an abscess around the valve ring. Which is the most appropriate next step?
opts: Correct. Abscess is an indication for surgery, alongside heart failure from valve dysfunction, infection not resolving on appropriate antibiotics and fungal infection, so cardiothoracic surgery evaluates her.
Waiting months allows the abscess to destroy tissue around the valve; abscess is an indication for surgery now.
Oral therapy is not appropriate; an abscess calls for surgical evaluation with continued parenteral antibiotics.
An abscess makes the infection complicated; shortening therapy is never appropriate here.

C.q: A 64-year-old woman with hypertension has a carotid bruit found on routine examination. She has never had neurologic symptoms. Duplex shows 35% stenosis. Which is the most appropriate management?
opts: Correct. Medical management is advised for symptomatic and asymptomatic patients with low-grade stenosis under 50%: antiplatelet therapy, control of hypertension, diabetes and lipids, smoking cessation, diet, exercise and weight reduction.
Endarterectomy is reserved for symptomatic stenosis over 70% or asymptomatic stenosis over 80% with a life expectancy over five years. A 35% stenosis is managed medically.
Stenting is an alternative revascularization for poor surgical candidates who meet surgical thresholds. A 35% asymptomatic stenosis needs medical management.
Digital subtraction angiography is used to guide interventions, and none is indicated here. Low-grade stenosis under 50% is managed medically.

C.q: Which aortic condition can also shed emboli that cause blue toe syndrome?
opts: A femoral pseudoaneurysm presents with pain from swelling or nerve compression. Abdominal aortic aneurysm is the listed embolic source.
Correct. A symptomatic, unruptured abdominal aortic aneurysm can produce embolic phenomena leading to blue toe syndrome, besides pain, early satiety and groin pain.
Carotid emboli go to the brain and eye. Abdominal aortic aneurysm can shed emboli to the toes.
Regurgitation is a valve leak, not an embolic source here. Abdominal aortic aneurysm can cause embolic blue toe.

C.q: A 38-year-old woman with obstructive hypertrophic cardiomyopathy still has disabling breathlessness despite a beta blocker and later verapamil. Echocardiogram shows systolic anterior motion (the anterior mitral leaflet pulled into the outflow tract) with mitral regurgitation. Which is the most appropriate next step?
opts: Diuretics lower preload and can worsen obstruction; they are used only with caution. Symptoms refractory to medication are treated with septal myectomy.

Correct. Surgical myectomy excises part of the septal myocardium causing outflow obstruction, and the mitral regurgitation from systolic anterior motion may resolve with myectomy alone, without valve replacement.
A permanent pacemaker treats conduction disease such as heart block. Refractory outflow obstruction is relieved by removing septal muscle with myectomy or alcohol septal ablation.
Nitrates reduce preload and afterload and aggravate outflow tract obstruction, so they are avoided. Refractory obstruction goes on to septal reduction by myectomy.

C.q: A 66-year-old woman with chronic obstructive lung disease is admitted with an exacerbation. She is confused, and the monitor shows runs of skipped beats from frequent early, wide QRS complexes without P waves. Her arterial oxygen tension is low. Which underlying problem should be corrected first?
opts: Correct. Hypoxemia is a main cause of premature ventricular contractions, along with electrolyte imbalance, so her low oxygen should be corrected first.
Blood pressure is not the named trigger. Hypoxemia and electrolyte imbalance are the main causes of premature ventricular contractions.
Temperature is not the named trigger. Hypoxemia, with electrolyte imbalance, drives premature ventricular contractions.
Blood glucose is not a named trigger. Her low oxygen tension is the cause to correct first.

C.q: A 44-year-old man began having pleuritic (worse with a deep breath) pericardial pain 8 weeks ago. Despite treatment the symptoms have never fully gone away, with no symptom-free interval. Which term best describes his course?
opts: Recurrence needs a symptom-free interval of 4 to 6 weeks or longer before symptoms return; he has had no such interval.
ruled out by a stated finding
Correct. Symptoms persisting beyond 4 to 6 weeks and up to 3 months without a sustained remission define incessant pericarditis; past 3 months the label becomes chronic.
Chronic pericarditis requires symptoms for more than 3 months. At 8 weeks without remission the course is incessant.
ruled out by a stated finding
Effusive-constrictive pericarditis is persistent constriction after an effusion is drained, a structural diagnosis, not a time label.

C.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following pericardial disease: 2. C.q: A 45-year-old woman taking warfarin for a mechanical valve presents with 2 days of sharp chest pain eased by leaning forward, widespread ST elevation and a small effusion. She is afebrile and her blood pressure is 128/78. Which is the most appropriate disposition?
opts: Oral anticoagulation is one of the features associated with higher risk and a potential need for hospitalization, so clinic follow-up alone is not enough here.
ruled out by a stated finding
Delaying evaluation is unsafe for a high-risk patient; anticoagulant use favors hospital admission now.

Correct. Patients on oral anticoagulants are among the higher-risk groups for acute pericarditis (with fever, subacute course, tamponade signs, large effusion, immunosuppression, trauma, raised troponin) and potentially need hospitalization.
Discharge after one dose of ibuprofen
A single dose and discharge ignores her high-risk status on anticoagulation, which raises the danger of bleeding into the pericardium.

Paroxysmal supraventricular tachycardia
C.q: A 71-year-old man with severe chronic obstructive pulmonary disease is admitted with an exacerbation and respiratory failure. His pulse is 128 and irregular. The electrocardiogram shows a P wave before every QRS, with at least three different P-wave shapes in lead II. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Atrial fibrillation is irregularly irregular with no P waves at all; his rhythm has a P wave before every QRS, in three shapes.
ruled out by a stated finding
Flutter shows uniform sawtooth waves at 250 or more; his discrete P waves in three different shapes point to multifocal atrial tachycardia.
Focal atrial tachycardia is regular, with one consistent abnormal P wave from a single focus, not three shapes.
ruled out by a stated finding

Correct. An irregular tachycardia with a P wave for every QRS and at least three distinct P-wave shapes in one lead is multifocal atrial tachycardia, usually from severe lung disease or heart failure in an acutely ill patient.

C.q: A 75-year-old man with peripheral artery disease has a hard, dry, black distal toe with a clear line between healthy and dead tissue. There is no swelling, moisture or fever. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Wet gangrene is moist and edematous with blistering and bacterial infection, and is a surgical emergency. This toe is hard, dry and clearly demarcated.
Gas gangrene is a wet gangrene from spore-forming clostridial species releasing toxins and gas. A dry, demarcated toe without fever is dry gangrene.
Correct. Dry gangrene has a hard, dry texture, usually involves the distal toes, shows clear demarcation between healthy and necrotic tissue, and is common in patients with peripheral artery disease.
Atheroembolism causes painful blue toes with palpable pulses from cholesterol debris. A hard, black, mummified toe with clear demarcation is dry gangrene.

C.q: In unstable Mobitz type II block, when medications are not used or do not work, which is the emergent measure?
opts: Synchronized cardioversion treats unstable tachycardias with a pulse. A failing conduction system with a slow rate needs pacing, not a shock.
Defibrillation is for ventricular fibrillation and pulseless ventricular tachycardia. Unstable Mobitz type II block is paced transcutaneously.
Vagal maneuvers slow atrioventricular conduction and would worsen a block. The emergent measure is transcutaneous pacing.
Correct. Transcutaneous pacing, with pads on the chest, is the emergent measure for unstable Mobitz type II block; it bridges the patient to a permanent pacemaker.

C.q: A 38-year-old woman has three months of worsening breathlessness on exertion and ankle swelling. Dilated cardiomyopathy is suspected, but her 12-lead electrocardiogram is completely normal. Which interpretation of the normal tracing is most accurate?
opts: It is what most dilated cardiomyopathy shows
The opposite holds: the electrocardiogram is usually abnormal in dilated cardiomyopathy, with arrhythmias or conduction delay such as left bundle branch block.
It excludes every cause of heart failure
A normal electrocardiogram cannot exclude heart failure in general. The test that excludes heart failure is a B-type natriuretic peptide below 100 pg/mL.
It makes dilated cardiomyopathy very unlikely

Correct. The electrocardiogram is usually abnormal in dilated cardiomyopathy, showing atrial fibrillation, premature ventricular contractions or left bundle branch block, so a normal tracing almost rules the diagnosis out.
It points to restrictive disease instead
Restrictive cardiomyopathy commonly shows atrial fibrillation, bundle branch blocks or low voltage in amyloidosis, so a normal tracing does not point toward it.

C.q: An 86-year-old woman with end-stage cardiomyopathy has breathlessness at rest, edema and fatigue despite maximal tolerated therapy. She is not a transplant or device candidate and says she wants comfort at home. Which is the most appropriate next step?
opts: She is not a device candidate, and her stated goal is comfort at home. Advance care planning and hospice referral match end-stage disease here.
She is not a transplant candidate and has asked for comfort at home. End-stage cardiomyopathy in this setting calls for goals-of-care discussion and hospice referral.
Discuss goals of care and hospice

Correct. Palliative care in cardiomyopathy covers symptom management of dyspnea, fatigue and edema, advance care planning and goals-of-care discussions, support for caregivers, and hospice referral in end-stage disease.
Stop all of her symptom medicines
Palliative care actively manages dyspnea, fatigue and edema; it does not withdraw symptom relief. The step now is goals-of-care discussion and hospice referral.

C.q: An 81-year-old man has known tachy-brady syndrome (a fast rhythm alternating with slow rates and pauses) and asks which fast rhythm is behind his palpitations. An ambulatory monitor is arranged. Which rhythm is it most likely to record during the fast episodes?
opts: Ventricular tachycardia can occur in some patients, who then need a defibrillator with the pacemaker, but atrial fibrillation is the most common.
A junctional rhythm is slow and regular, usually 40 to 60, not the fast phase of tachy-brady syndrome.
Flutter is an organized atrial circuit with sawtooth waves; it is not the usual fast rhythm of tachy-brady syndrome.
Correct. In tachy-brady syndrome the tachyarrhythmia that alternates with bradycardia or pauses is most commonly atrial fibrillation.

C.q: A 53-year-old man on the cardiology ward develops jugular venous distension and a blood pressure of 88/60 a day after a catheter procedure. Before drainage, which bedside triad should be specifically checked for?
opts: Correct. The Beck triad is decreased arterial pressure, distended jugular veins and distant (muffled) heart sounds, the three bedside signs of cardiac tamponade to check before drainage.
The Kussmaul sign and the knock belong to constriction, so this mixture is not the tamponade triad.
Hypertension, bradycardia and irregular breathing are the Cushing reflex of raised intracranial pressure.
Fever, a new murmur and splinters
Fever, a new murmur and splinter hemorrhages suggest infective endocarditis, not tamponade.

C.q: A 26-year-old man with suspected viral myocarditis has an elevated troponin and normal coronary arteries. His cardiologist wants to see how much of the heart muscle is inflamed without an invasive procedure. Which test shows the extent of inflammation?
opts: Right heart catheterization with pressure tracings
Pressure tracings help evaluate restrictive physiology. Inflammation is shown noninvasively by gadolinium-enhanced magnetic resonance imaging.
Correct. Gadolinium-enhanced magnetic resonance imaging is part of the myocarditis work-up because the gadolinium improves visibility of the inflammation and shows its extent.
Exercise echocardiography assesses functional capacity, ischemia and obstruction in hypertrophic cardiomyopathy. It does not show the extent of inflammation.
Ambulatory rhythm monitoring for forty-eight hours
Ambulatory monitoring detects arrhythmias and grades sudden death risk, most notably in hypertrophic cardiomyopathy. It cannot show inflamed heart muscle.

C.q: A 34-year-old woman without diabetes has ulcers on the posterior aspect of both lower legs. Her pedal pulses are strong, and there are no varicose veins, brown pigmentation or leg swelling. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Arterial ulcers are painful, usually lateral at the ankle, and come with weak pulses. Her strong pulses and posterior, bilateral distribution point to erythema induratum.
Venous ulcers sit above the medial or anterior ankle with edema, brown pigmentation and varicosities. Bilateral posterior lower leg ulcers without these changes suggest erythema induratum.
Correct. Bilateral ulcers on the posterior aspect of the lower leg, with intact pulses and no venous skin changes, is the pattern listed for erythema induratum in the differential of leg ulcers.
Neuropathic ulcers follow diabetic nerve damage and she has no diabetes. Bilateral ulcers on the back of the lower legs are the pattern of erythema induratum.

opts: Reflux disease is not a cause of bundle branch block. Pulmonary hypertension is.
Osteoporosis has no link to cardiac conduction. Pulmonary hypertension is the named cause of right bundle branch block.
Correct. Pulmonary hypertension is a named cause of right bundle branch block, by chronically straining the right ventricle and its conduction system.
Raynaud phenomenon affects digital vessels, not cardiac conduction. Pulmonary hypertension is the named cause.

C.q: A 28-year-old woman with a stab wound to the abdomen arrives pulseless after losing a large amount of blood. The monitor shows an organized narrow rhythm. Compressions are underway. Besides compressions and epinephrine, which problem must be addressed urgently?
opts: Hypothermia is a reversible cause, but nothing points to it. Hypovolemia from bleeding is the urgent problem.
Correct. The two leading causes of pulseless electrical activity in adults are hypovolemia and hypoxia; her massive blood loss is hypovolemia that must be corrected.
Nothing suggests a toxin. Her massive blood loss means hypovolemia, a leading cause of pulseless electrical activity.
Hyperkalemia is a reversible cause of arrest, but her picture is hemorrhage. Hypovolemia is the leading cause to address.

C.q: A 67-year-old man with atrial fibrillation is being discharged after treatment of an embolic leg occlusion. Which warning symptoms should prompt him to return immediately?
opts: Dry, shiny skin on the shins
Dry, shiny, hairless skin is a chronic sign of diminished flow in peripheral artery disease. Recurrent embolism announces itself with sudden pain, pallor, coldness and numbness.
Mild ankle swelling in the evening
Evening ankle swelling suggests venous insufficiency, not arterial occlusion. The return warnings are the six P's: pain, pallor, pulselessness, paresthesia, paralysis, poikilothermia.
Correct. The six P's of arterial assessment (pain, pallor, pulselessness, paresthesia, paralysis and poikilothermia) mark acute limb ischemia, a vascular emergency that needs immediate care.
Exertional calf cramping relieved by rest is intermittent claudication, a chronic symptom. A recurrent embolus presents with sudden pain, pallor, coldness and numbness.

C.q: A 66-year-old man has a continuous bruit and a palpable thrill (a vibration felt over the skin) over the left femoral region, with mild leg swelling. He has not had dialysis and has no trauma history. His only recent procedure was an endovascular repair of an iliac artery performed through the left groin. Which is the most likely cause?
opts: Correct. Lower extremity arteriovenous fistulas are most commonly iatrogenic, caused by use of the groin femoral vessels for percutaneous arterial and venous access during endovascular procedures.
Congenital fistulas exist from birth and often have numerous communications. A new bruit after groin access in an adult points to an acquired, iatrogenic origin.
Superficial reflux causes varicose veins and chronic venous insufficiency, not a continuous bruit with thrill. A new artery to vein communication follows the groin puncture.
Created fistulas are made for hemodialysis and are usually in the upper arm or forearm. This man has no dialysis history and the fistula sits at the femoral puncture.

C.q: Which electrocardiogram changes occur in Takotsubo (stress) cardiomyopathy?
opts: Left bundle branch block is the conduction delay described in dilated cardiomyopathy.
Low QRS voltage in all leads
Low QRS voltage suggests amyloid infiltration in restrictive cardiomyopathy, not stress cardiomyopathy.
Prominent inferior and lateral Q waves reflect septal hypertrophy in hypertrophic cardiomyopathy.
ST elevation and T wave inversion
Correct. The electrocardiogram shows ST segment elevation and T wave inversion, which is why the syndrome is managed like acute coronary syndrome until catheterization.

C.q: A 63-year-old man has an incidental 4.0 cm ascending thoracic aortic aneurysm on a chest radiograph and follow-up imaging. He has no symptoms. Which surveillance plan is appropriate?
opts: Abdominal ultrasound every three years with no other imaging
Three-yearly ultrasound is the plan for small abdominal aneurysms and cannot see the thoracic aorta. His surveillance is computed tomography or magnetic resonance.
Computed tomography or magnetic resonance every 3 to 5 years
Correct. Thoracic aneurysms under 4.5 cm are followed with computed tomography or magnetic resonance imaging every three to five years; 4.5 to 5.4 cm moves to every six to 12 months.
Computed tomography or magnetic resonance every 6 to 12 months
Six-to-12-monthly imaging applies to thoracic aneurysms of 4.5 to 5.4 cm. At 4.0 cm the interval is every three to five years.
Open repair with aortic root replacement within the month
Asymptomatic ascending repair is generally indicated above 5.5 cm or with growth over 0.5 cm per year. At 4.0 cm he needs surveillance, not surgery.

C.q: A 57-year-old man survives an out-of-hospital cardiac arrest from pulseless ventricular tachycardia. After stabilization no reversible cause is found. Which device is most appropriate before discharge?
opts: A pacemaker treats slow, blocked rhythms. Survivors of ventricular tachycardia arrest need a defibrillator.
A biventricular pacer treats symptomatic left bundle branch block with reduced ejection fraction. Arrest survivors need a defibrillator.
Correct. Once stabilized after life-threatening ventricular tachycardia or fibrillation, most patients need an implantable cardioverter defibrillator for secondary prevention of sudden cardiac death.
A loop recorder only records the rhythm. He needs a device that detects and shocks lethal rhythms.

C.io: Identify medical care strategies for pericardial disease in the lecture topic list for the following populations. 9. adult 10. elderly
C.q: Why is a nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug approached with caution in older adults with pericarditis?
opts: It appears on the Beers list
Correct. In older adults, nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs appear on the Beers list of potentially inappropriate medications and call for caution; colchicine may need a dose reduction.
Drug-induced lupus comes from procainamide and hydralazine, not from these drugs. The caution in older adults is their place on the Beers list.
It raises the risk of tamponade
Anti-inflammatory therapy treats the inflammation rather than causing tamponade. The caution in older adults is the Beers list.
QT prolongation is not the concern named for these drugs. Their place on the Beers list, for bleeding and kidney risk in older adults, is.

C.q: A 69-year-old woman being evaluated for endocarditis had a soft systolic murmur documented for 10 years. Today the murmur sounds a little louder. How does this change count under the modified Duke criteria?
opts: Only new valvular regurgitation meets the criterion; a louder preexisting murmur is specifically not sufficient.
A louder old murmur adds nothing toward the major criterion and cannot confirm the diagnosis.
Immunologic phenomena are glomerulonephritis, Osler nodes, Roth spots and rheumatoid factor, not murmur changes.
It does not meet the major criterion
Correct. New valvular regurgitation counts as endocardial involvement, but an increase or change in a preexisting murmur is not sufficient.

C.q: A 63-year-old woman is diagnosed with constrictive pericarditis. She had mantle-field radiotherapy for Hodgkin lymphoma 25 years ago and is otherwise well. Which feature of her history most worsens her long-term prognosis?
opts: Sex is not named as a determinant of survival. Prior ionizing radiation carries the worst prognosis.
Comorbidities worsen the outlook, so their absence helps. Her prior radiation is what worsens it.
The lymphoma itself is cured; it is the radiation used to treat it that predicts the worst survival.
Correct. Etiology is an important determinant of survival in constrictive pericarditis, and prior ionizing radiation is associated with the worst survival rates.

C.q: A 54-year-old woman who started a new antibiotic three days ago faints briefly. Her electrocardiogram before the event showed a markedly prolonged QT. The monitor now shows a wide QRS tachycardia whose peaks rise and fall so that the complexes seem to twist around the baseline. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Correct. Polymorphic ventricular tachycardia whose QRS complexes appear to twist around the baseline, on a background of a long QT, is torsades de pointes; most cases come from acquired long QT, often drug-induced.
Atrial flutter has sawtooth atrial waves and narrow QRS complexes. A wide twisting rhythm with a long QT is torsades.
Monomorphic ventricular tachycardia keeps one QRS shape. Complexes that twist around the baseline with a long QT are torsades.
Fibrillation is chaotic, uncoordinated activity with no organized QRS. Twisting, rising and falling complexes are torsades.

C.io: Identify medical care strategies for infective endocarditis for the following populations. 8. infant 9. child 10. adolescent 11. adult 12. elderly
C.q: A 6-year-old with repaired congenital heart disease has 3 weeks of low-grade fever, fatigue, joint aches and weight loss. A new murmur is heard. Which organism most commonly causes endocarditis in this age group?
opts: Enterococci are less common in children than in adults; viridans streptococci lead after age 1 with congenital heart disease.
Correct. Children over 1 year with congenital heart disease develop indolent viridans group streptococcal disease; Staphylococcus aureus comes next.
Group B streptococci are a less common neonatal organism, not the leading organism after age 1.
Candida is tied to neonatal central lines and hyperalimentation, not indolent disease in older children.

D.q: A 74-year-old woman with recurrent urinary tract infections was treated for pyelonephritis a month ago. She now has low-grade fevers, fatigue and a new murmur, and blood cultures grow gram-positive cocci. Which organism is most likely?
opts: Coagulase-negative staphylococci such as Staphylococcus epidermidis are skin organisms tied to early prosthetic valve and device infection, not urinary sources.
Correct. The genitourinary tract is the source of enterococci, which cause subacute and native valve endocarditis; urinary tract infection gives them a route into the blood.
Viridans streptococci come from the oral cavity; a genitourinary source points to enterococci.
Streptococcus gallolyticus comes from the gastrointestinal tract. The urinary source organism is enterococci.

D.q: A 74-year-old man with advanced dilated cardiomyopathy has refractory symptoms on full medical therapy. Severe lung disease and frailty rule him out as a transplant candidate, and he wants to remain at home and mobile. Which treatment option fits his situation?
opts: Assist device as a bridge to transplant
Bridge therapy supports a patient until transplantation or recovery. He cannot receive a transplant, so the device would be permanent destination therapy.

Correct. Destination therapy with a left ventricular assist device is for patients who are not candidates for cardiac transplantation. Patients may live more than five years with the device and can stay mobile.
Myectomy relieves septal outflow obstruction in hypertrophic cardiomyopathy and does nothing for a dilated, weak ventricle. Destination assist-device therapy fits him.
He has already been ruled out as a transplant candidate. For such patients the left ventricular assist device is used as destination therapy.

D.q: A 19-year-old swimmer has an electrocardiogram before a sports physical. She has no symptoms. The rate is 72, with a normal P wave before every narrow QRS, but the beats come closer together as she breathes in and spread apart as she breathes out. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Multifocal atrial tachycardia is a fast, irregular rhythm with at least three P-wave shapes in acutely ill lung or heart patients; her single P-wave shape at 72 is sinus.
Atrial fibrillation is irregularly irregular with no P waves; she has a normal P wave before every beat and a regular pattern tied to breathing.

Correct. A normal P wave before every narrow QRS at 60 to 100, with the rate rising on inspiration and falling on expiration, is sinus arrhythmia: a normal, physiologic rhythm that is irregular with a pattern.
Sick sinus syndrome produces pauses, sinus arrest or tachy-brady swings in a diseased node, usually with symptoms; a breathing-linked variation in a healthy swimmer is sinus arrhythmia.

D.q: Which medication is a recognized cause of pericardial effusion?
opts: Amlodipine is not a listed cause of pericardial effusion. Doxorubicin, minoxidil and phenytoin are.
Metformin is not among the medication causes of pericardial effusion, which include doxorubicin, minoxidil and phenytoin.
Correct. Medication causes of pericardial effusion include doxorubicin, minoxidil, phenytoin, and hydralazine and procainamide through drug-induced lupus.
Levothyroxine treats hypothyroidism, and myxedema is itself a cause of effusion; the drug is not a cause. Doxorubicin is a listed medication cause.

D.q: Stable atrial fibrillation with rapid ventricular response is treated how?
opts: Mapping and ablation is a later, elective rhythm option, not the acute treatment of rapid ventricular response.
Synchronized cardioversion is for the unstable patient; a stable patient in rapid ventricular response is rate-controlled intravenously.
Atropine speeds the heart and treats unstable bradycardia; it would worsen rapid ventricular response.
Correct. A hemodynamically stable patient in rapid ventricular response gets intravenous rate control; a stable patient without it gets rate control by mouth.

D.q: A 69-year-old woman in stable, rate-controlled atrial flutter of unknown duration is to have elective outpatient cardioversion. Which must come first?
opts: Ablation is the definitive alternative to cardioversion, not a step before it; anticoagulation comes first.
Correct. Outpatient cardioversion of atrial flutter is done after 21 days of anticoagulation, and anticoagulation is part of flutter management.
Adenosine does not prepare a patient for cardioversion; three weeks of anticoagulation does.
A pacemaker treats slow rhythms and is not a prerequisite for cardioversion; 21 days of anticoagulation is.

D.q: A 64-year-old woman has been in the hospital for 2 weeks with a peripherally inserted central line. She develops fever, and two separate blood cultures grow a gram-positive coccus with no other source. Which organism causes the largest share of this setting's native valve endocarditis?
opts: Enterococci cause about 16% of health care-associated native valve endocarditis, far behind Staphylococcus aureus.
Coagulase-negative staphylococci cause about 11% of health care-associated native valve endocarditis, well behind Staphylococcus aureus at about 52%.
Correct. Staphylococcus aureus causes about 52% of health care-associated native valve endocarditis, and methicillin resistance is common among these strains.
Streptococci as a group lead community-acquired disease (about 40%) but cause only about 13% of health care-associated native valve endocarditis.

D.q: An elevated D-dimer implies increased activity of which process?
opts: Correct. An elevated D-dimer implies increased fibrinolysis, the breakdown of fibrin clot; it can occur in a deep vein thrombosis but also in many other conditions.
Platelet production is measured by the platelet count. D-dimer reflects increased fibrinolysis, the breakdown of fibrin.
Hemolysis is followed with bilirubin and reticulocytes. D-dimer reflects increased fibrinolysis.
Vitamin K deficiency is tracked by clotting times such as the international normalized ratio. D-dimer reflects increased fibrinolysis.

D.q: A 72-year-old woman had a bioprosthetic aortic valve placed 5 months ago. She now has a fever of 39.0 °C (102.2 °F) and a new regurgitant murmur, and blood cultures have been drawn. Which empiric regimen is most appropriate?
opts: Ceftriaxone alone misses methicillin-resistant staphylococci, which must be covered empirically, especially early after valve surgery.
Vancomycin plus ceftriaxone is for native valves, subacute presentations and prosthetic valves in place more than a year.
Penicillin G with gentamicin is directed therapy for viridans streptococci once identified, not empiric therapy for an early prosthetic valve.
Correct. When a prosthetic valve has been in place for 1 year or less, empiric therapy is vancomycin plus gentamicin plus cefepime.

D.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following arterial occlusive disease and aortic aneurysm: 2. Arterial thrombosis/embolism 3. Peripheral artery disease 4. Carotid artery disease 5. Aortic aneurysms 6. Aortic dissection
D.q: A 70-year-old man has an asymptomatic infrarenal abdominal aortic aneurysm measuring 3.4 cm on ultrasound. Which follow-up is most appropriate?
opts: Every identified aneurysm needs routine follow-up of size and growth rate. At 3.4 cm that means ultrasound every three years.
Elective repair is for 5.0 cm or larger in women and over 5.5 cm in men, or rapid growth. A 3.4 cm aneurysm needs surveillance, every three years.
Ultrasound or computed tomography every six to 12 months is for aneurysms of 4.0 to 5.4 cm. At 3.4 cm the interval is every three years.
Correct. Once identified, an aneurysm is followed for size and growth; a 3.0 to 3.9 cm aneurysm is imaged with ultrasound every three years.

D.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following cardiomyopathies: 2. Restrictive cardiomyopathy 3. Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy 4. Dilated cardiomyopathy 5. Stress cardiomyopathy 6. Myocarditis
D.q: A 58-year-old woman received mediastinal radiation and chemotherapy for a chest cancer 15 years ago. She now has progressive exercise intolerance, orthopnea (breathlessness lying flat), ascites and swollen legs. Echocardiogram shows stiff ventricles of normal size, marked atrial enlargement and abnormal diastolic function with a preserved ejection fraction. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Myocarditis follows a recent viral prodrome with acute heart failure and raised troponin. A slow course years after radiation with stiff ventricles is restrictive disease.
Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy is inherited, with an asymmetric thick septum and outflow murmur. Treatment-related fibrosis with big atria is restrictive cardiomyopathy.

Correct. Mediastinal radiation and chemotherapy cause inflammation and then fibrosis that restricts filling, and a prior history of radiation or chemotherapy is a named clue in restrictive cardiomyopathy.
Chemotherapy can also cause dilated cardiomyopathy, but that gives dilated, thin walls with a reduced ejection fraction. Stiff, normal-sized ventricles with big atria are restrictive.

D.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following atrial and supraventricular dysrhythmias: a. Paroxysmal supraventricular tachycardia
D.q: A 40-year-old woman has a regular narrow complex tachycardia at 182 with palpitations and mild anxiety. Her blood pressure is 128/80, oxygen saturation 98%, and she is alert without chest pain. Which treatment should be tried first?
opts: Synchronized cardioversion is reserved for the unstable patient; she is stable, so a vagal maneuver comes first.
Correct. Stable supraventricular tachycardia is treated first with a vagal maneuver, then adenosine (up to twice), keeping synchronized cardioversion for instability.
Adenosine comes second, after a vagal maneuver fails, in stable supraventricular tachycardia.
Amiodarone is tried for chemical cardioversion of focal atrial tachycardia, not as the first step in a stable narrow complex tachycardia.

D.q: A 74-year-old man with sudden leg ischemia has sensory loss extending beyond the toes with rest pain, mild-to-moderate weakness, an inaudible arterial Doppler signal and an audible venous signal. Where should his evaluation and treatment take place?
opts: Outpatient testing wastes the time this limb does not have. Sensory loss beyond the toes with weakness means immediate revascularization in a surgical suite.
Amputation is for irreversible limbs with profound sensory loss, paralysis and absent venous signals. This limb is still salvageable with immediate revascularization.
Time for imaging such as computed tomography angiography belongs to viable or marginally threatened limbs. An immediately threatened limb goes to the surgical suite.
In the surgical suite, without delay
Correct. An immediately threatened limb is salvageable only with immediate revascularization, so it should preferentially undergo further evaluation and treatment in a surgical suite.

D.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following: 2. Acute endocarditis 3. Subacute endocarditis
D.q: A 64-year-old man will finish 5 more weeks of intravenous antibiotics for endocarditis after discharge. Which consultant manages his antibiotic therapy and outpatient monitoring?
opts: Cardiothoracic surgery evaluates surgery and anticoagulation needs, not the outpatient antibiotic plan.
Correct. Infectious disease manages antibiotic therapy and outpatient monitoring pending disposition, as part of the multidisciplinary team.
Addiction medicine provides harm reduction for people who inject drugs, not antibiotic monitoring.
Dermatology has no listed role in endocarditis antibiotic management; infectious disease directs the antibiotic plan.

D.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following pericardial disease: 2. Pericarditis 3. Acute 4. Recurrent 5. Constrictive pericarditis 6. Pericardial effusion 7. Cardiac tamponade
D.q: A 40-year-old woman has taken ibuprofen and colchicine for 8 days for presumed viral pericarditis. She still has a temperature of 38.5 degrees Celsius and pleuritic (worse with a deep breath) pain, and a new pericardial effusion has appeared on echocardiogram. Which is the most appropriate next step?
opts: Continue the same drugs for a month
Continuing unchanged ignores treatment failure. No response by 1 week calls for admission and a search for a specific cause.
Start anakinra as a first step
Anakinra is for recurrent, colchicine-resistant or steroid-dependent disease with an inflammatory phenotype; first she needs a search for a specific cause.
Admit and look for another cause

Correct. Persistent fever and pain with a new effusion define treatment failure, and failure to respond within 1 week suggests a cause other than idiopathic or viral; no improvement after 7 days favors hospitalization.
Stop colchicine and add a diuretic
Diuretics treat fluid overload in constriction, and stopping colchicine removes useful therapy. She needs evaluation for another cause.

D.io: Discuss indications and antibiotic regimens for subacute bacterial endocarditis prophylaxis.
D.q: When is the dental prophylaxis dose given?
opts: Prophylaxis is a single dose, not a month of daily antibiotics; it is given 30-60 minutes before the procedure.
Correct. The single prophylactic dose is given 30-60 minutes before the procedure, so the drug is circulating when the transient bacteremia occurs.
A dose a week early would be gone by the procedure. It is given 30-60 minutes beforehand.
A dose after the procedure misses the bacteremia it is meant to prevent; it is given 30-60 minutes before.

D.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following: 2. Acute endocarditis 3. Subacute endocarditis
D.q: A 44-year-old man arrives with a temperature of 40.2 °C (104.4 °F), rigors and a new murmur, and he looks toxic. Acute endocarditis is suspected. Which is the most appropriate next step?
opts: Antibiotics given before cultures can leave them negative and lose the organism; cultures come first.
Two cultures within 1-2 hours, then antibiotics
Correct. If the presentation suggests acute endocarditis, two cultures are drawn within the first 1-2 hours, and empiric antibiotics are started only after the cultures are drawn.
Echocardiography matters, but the first step in a toxic patient is cultures within 1-2 hours, then empiric antibiotics.
Untreated acute endocarditis can be fatal within weeks and destroys valves rapidly; observation is not appropriate.

D.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following ventricular dysrhythmias: a. Atrioventricular block b. Bundle branch blocks c. Ventricular premature beats d. Ventricular tachycardia e. Ventricular fibrillation f. Torsades de Pointes g. Idioventricular rhythm h. Junctional rhythm i. QT prolongation
D.q: A 58-year-old man collapses in a gym. He is unresponsive, not breathing and has no pulse. The monitor shows chaotic, irregular waves of varying size with no identifiable QRS complexes. Which rhythm is present?
opts: Correct. Uncoordinated electrical activity with no rate, no P waves and no organized QRS, in a pulseless patient, is ventricular fibrillation.
Asystole is a flat line with no electrical activity. Chaotic waves mean ventricular fibrillation.
Polymorphic ventricular tachycardia still has identifiable, if varying, QRS complexes. Chaotic waves without any QRS are fibrillation.
Pulseless electrical activity shows an organized rhythm without a pulse. This rhythm is chaotic.

D.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following arterial occlusive disease and aortic aneurysm: 2. Arterial thrombosis/embolism 3. Peripheral artery disease 4. Carotid artery disease 5. Aortic aneurysms 6. Aortic dissection
D.q: A 79-year-old man with multiple serious medical conditions is a poor surgical candidate. He had a transient ischemic attack and has a 90% symptomatic carotid stenosis. Which intervention is most appropriate?
opts: Medical management alone is advised for stenosis under 50%. A symptomatic 90% stenosis warrants revascularization, here by stenting because surgery is high risk.
Correct. Carotid angioplasty with stenting, most often through the common femoral artery, is less invasive and allows intervention in poor surgical candidates with a qualifying stenosis.
Angiography guides an intervention but does not treat the stenosis. A poor surgical candidate with this stenosis is treated with carotid stenting.
Endarterectomy is the gold standard for high-grade stenosis but requires open surgery. For a poor surgical candidate, the less invasive stenting approach is chosen.

Paroxysmal supraventricular tachycardia
D.q: A 38-year-old woman notices occasional skipped beats during a stressful month of heavy coffee and wine. Her electrocardiogram shows occasional early beats with an abnormally shaped P wave and a narrow QRS, and her examination and echocardiogram are normal. Which advice is most appropriate?
opts: Anticoagulation is for atrial fibrillation and flutter; isolated premature atrial beats need none.
A beta blocker is for persistent, symptomatic premature atrial contractions after triggers are addressed, not the first response.
Correct. Premature atrial contractions in a normal heart with excess alcohol, stress or caffeine are benign: counsel avoidance of precipitants and reassure about the benign nature of the rhythm.
Ablation is for frequent premature atrial contractions or those triggering atrial fibrillation; hers are occasional and benign.

D.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following atrial and supraventricular dysrhythmias: a. Sinus arrhythmia b. Sinus bradycardia c. Sinus tachycardia d. Sick sinus syndrome e. Atrial premature beats f. Atrial flutter g. Atrial fibrillation h. Atrial tachycardia i. Paroxysmal supraventricular tachycardia
D.q: A 17-year-old basketball player collapses briefly during a game and recovers. In the emergency department he is in sinus rhythm at 78. His electrocardiogram shows a PR interval of 0.10 seconds and a delta wave (a slurred upstroke at the start of the QRS) with a widened QRS. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Correct. A short PR interval with a delta wave and widened QRS in sinus rhythm is pre-excitation from an accessory pathway (the bundle of Kent): Wolff-Parkinson-White, which classically first shows itself as collapse in a young athlete.
Nodal reentry is a circuit inside the atrioventricular node and does not produce a short PR or delta wave in sinus rhythm.
Sick sinus syndrome causes pauses and tachy-brady swings in older adults; it does not produce a delta wave.
Focal atrial tachycardia gives a fast rhythm with an abnormal P wave; it does not shorten the PR interval or create a delta wave in sinus rhythm.

D.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following: 2. Acute endocarditis 3. Subacute endocarditis
D.q: Which disorder in the differential of infective endocarditis causes thromboemboli and cardiac valve disease?
opts: Lyme disease enters the differential through fever and, rarely, myocarditis, not through thromboemboli and valve disease.
Polymyalgia rheumatica causes myalgia and raised inflammatory markers, not thromboemboli and valve disease.
Correct. Antiphospholipid syndrome causes thromboemboli and cardiac valve disease, so it can imitate the embolic picture of infective endocarditis.
Meningitis mimics endocarditis with fever and rash. Thromboemboli plus valve disease point to antiphospholipid syndrome.

D.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following ventricular dysrhythmias: a. Atrioventricular block b. Bundle branch blocks c. Ventricular premature beats d. Ventricular tachycardia e. Ventricular fibrillation f. Torsades de Pointes g. Idioventricular rhythm h. Junctional rhythm i. QT prolongation
D.q: A 66-year-old man with a large anterior myocardial infarction two years ago has palpitations and lightheadedness. He is alert, with a blood pressure of 112/70. The monitor shows a regular wide QRS rhythm at 170 per minute with no P waves, every complex the same shape, for over a minute. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Ventricular fibrillation is uncoordinated activity with no pulse. He is alert with a blood pressure, and the rhythm is organized.
Complete block gives a slow wide rhythm, usually below 40, with dissociated P waves. This rhythm is fast at 170.

Correct. A regular wide QRS rhythm of 100 to 250 per minute without P waves, with identical complexes lasting over 30 seconds, is sustained monomorphic ventricular tachycardia, often seen after myocardial infarction.
Polymorphic ventricular tachycardia has QRS complexes that vary in shape. Identical complexes make this monomorphic.

D.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following ventricular dysrhythmias: a. Atrioventricular block b. Bundle branch blocks c. Ventricular premature beats d. Ventricular tachycardia e. Ventricular fibrillation f. Torsades de Pointes g. Idioventricular rhythm h. Junctional rhythm i. QT prolongation
D.q: A 71-year-old man admitted with pneumonia develops frequent early, wide QRS beats with no preceding P wave on telemetry, and he feels his heart skipping. His oxygen saturation on the monitor is drifting down. Which is the most appropriate next step?
opts: Amiodarone is for ventricular tachycardia and fibrillation. Premature beats are addressed by finding and correcting hypoxemia or electrolytes.
Ablation is reserved for refractory symptoms or beat-induced cardiomyopathy. The first step is to correct hypoxemia and electrolytes.
Defibrillation is for ventricular fibrillation or pulseless ventricular tachycardia. He has isolated premature beats with a pulse.
Correct. Hypoxemia and electrolyte imbalance are the main causes of premature ventricular contractions, so new frequent beats call for checking oxygenation and electrolytes first.

D.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following pericardial disease: 2. Pericarditis 3. Acute 4. Recurrent 5. Constrictive pericarditis 6. Pericardial effusion 7. Cardiac tamponade
D.q: Which description fits recurrent pericarditis?
opts: Symptoms persist without remission for up to 3 months
Persistence without a sustained remission from 4 to 6 weeks up to 3 months is incessant pericarditis; recurrence needs a symptom-free gap first.
Symptoms persist without any remission past 3 months
Unbroken symptoms beyond 3 months define chronic pericarditis. Recurrence requires a symptom-free interval of 4 to 6 weeks or longer before the symptoms return.
Symptoms return after a symptom-free gap of 4 to 6 weeks
Correct. Recurrent pericarditis is when symptoms of acute pericarditis return after a symptom-free interval of 4 to 6 weeks or longer, which separates it from incessant disease.
Constriction persists after an effusion has been drained
Persistent constriction after drainage of an effusion is effusive-constrictive pericarditis. Recurrent pericarditis is a return of symptoms after a 4-to-6-week symptom-free gap.

D.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following ventricular dysrhythmias: a. Atrioventricular block b. Bundle branch blocks c. Ventricular premature beats d. Ventricular tachycardia e. Ventricular fibrillation f. Torsades de Pointes g. Idioventricular rhythm h. Junctional rhythm i. QT prolongation
D.q: A 52-year-old man on telemetry has a prolonged QT after starting a new medication and then develops polymorphic ventricular tachycardia (QRS complexes that vary in shape and twist around the baseline). He becomes unresponsive and pulseless. Which is the most appropriate next step?
opts: Synchronized shocks need a consistent QRS and a pulse. Pulseless polymorphic tachycardia is defibrillated.
ruled out by a stated finding
Pacing treats slow, blocked rhythms. A pulseless polymorphic tachycardia is defibrillated.
Magnesium breaks torsades in a conscious patient; a pulseless patient needs defibrillation first.
Correct. Pulseless polymorphic ventricular tachycardia, including torsades, is treated as cardiac arrest with defibrillation and cardiopulmonary resuscitation; magnesium follows.

D.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following venous disorders: 2. Deep vein thrombosis 3. Phlebitis a. Thrombophlebitis Septic thrombophlebitis 4. Arteriovenous fistula of the extremity a. Acquired (e.g. trauma, iatrogenic) b. Created (i.e. for hemodialysis) 5. Chronic venous insufficiency 6. Varicose veins
D.q: What most commonly causes a lower extremity arteriovenous fistula?
opts: Fistulas created for dialysis are placed in the upper arm or forearm, generally preferred over the leg. Lower extremity fistulas usually follow groin access.
Congenital fistulas exist but are not the most common lower extremity cause. Most follow iatrogenic groin access for endovascular procedures.
Trauma can cause an acquired fistula, but the most common lower extremity cause is iatrogenic injury from groin access during a procedure.
Correct. Lower extremity fistulas are most commonly iatrogenic, from using the groin (femoral vessels) for percutaneous arterial and venous access in endovascular procedures.

D.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following pericardial disease: 2. Pericarditis 3. Acute 4. Recurrent 5. Constrictive pericarditis 6. Pericardial effusion 7. Cardiac tamponade
D.q: A 38-year-old woman has her second recurrence of idiopathic pericarditis despite colchicine. Her temperature is 38.4 degrees Celsius, C-reactive protein is 45 mg/L, and cardiac magnetic resonance shows pericardial edema with late gadolinium enhancement. Which therapy is most appropriate to add?
opts: Surgery is considered for frequent, highly symptomatic recurrences with effusion or for constriction; this inflammatory phenotype calls for an interleukin-1 blocker first.
Intravenous immunoglobulin is a later-line option on the older treatment table. For colchicine-resistant recurrence with an inflammatory phenotype, anti-interleukin-1 therapy is preferred.
Azathioprine is a later-line immunosuppressant and not the preferred agent; anti-interleukin-1 therapy targets this inflammatory phenotype.

Correct. With an inflammatory phenotype (C-reactive protein above 10 mg/L, fever, imaging inflammation) and a colchicine-resistant second recurrence of idiopathic disease, an interleukin-1 blocker such as anakinra or rilonacept is added and now used earlier.

D.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following ventricular dysrhythmias: a. Atrioventricular block b. Bundle branch blocks c. Ventricular premature beats d. Ventricular tachycardia e. Ventricular fibrillation f. Torsades de Pointes g. Idioventricular rhythm h. Junctional rhythm i. QT prolongation
D.q: A 68-year-old man with Mobitz type II block found on a routine tracing declines a pacemaker because he feels perfectly well. Which risk should be explained to him?
opts: Atrial fibrillation is not the feared outcome. The risk is progression to complete heart block and sudden cardiac death.
Correct. Mobitz type II carries a higher risk of progression to complete heart block and sudden cardiac death, and it is considered dangerous even without symptoms.
Mobitz type II does not regress to a milder block; it tends to progress to complete heart block.
Mobitz type II does not resolve on its own; its risk is unpredictable progression to complete block and sudden death.

D.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following ventricular dysrhythmias: a. Atrioventricular block b. Bundle branch blocks c. Ventricular premature beats d. Ventricular tachycardia e. Ventricular fibrillation f. Torsades de Pointes g. Idioventricular rhythm h. Junctional rhythm i. QT prolongation
D.q: Which is the first treatment for torsades de pointes in a conscious patient?
opts: Correct. In a conscious patient, intravenous magnesium breaks torsades, followed by more magnesium as an infusion.
Procainamide prolongs the QT and is avoided in torsades. Intravenous magnesium is the first treatment.
Amiodarone prolongs the QT and is avoided in torsades. Intravenous magnesium is the first treatment.
Beta blockers are avoided in torsades because the slower rate lengthens the QT. Magnesium is given first.

D.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following arterial occlusive disease and aortic aneurysm: 2. Arterial thrombosis/embolism 3. Peripheral artery disease 4. Carotid artery disease 5. Aortic aneurysms 6. Aortic dissection
D.q: A 74-year-old man with diabetes who smokes wakes most nights with burning pain in his forefoot and toes that eases when he hangs the leg over the bed; he now sleeps in a recliner. Which ankle-brachial index range would be expected?
opts: The 0.4 to 0.9 band is claudication, pain with activity relieved by rest. Nocturnal rest pain relieved by dependency sits in the 0 to 0.4 band.
Above 0.9 up to 1.3 is normal, which cannot explain nightly ischemic pain. Rest pain matches an index of 0 to 0.4.
Correct. Rest pain and tissue loss (ulcer, gangrene) correspond to an ankle-brachial index of 0 to 0.4, the critical limb ischemia band, well below the claudication range.
Above 1.3 reflects calcified, noncompressible arteries and gives a falsely high value. The expected band for true ischemic rest pain is 0 to 0.4.
