D.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following cardiomyopathies: 2. Restrictive cardiomyopathy 3. Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy 4. Dilated cardiomyopathy 5. Stress cardiomyopathy 6. Myocarditis
D.q: A 23-year-old previously healthy man has breathlessness, chest pain and exercise intolerance ten days after a flulike illness with fever, myalgia and diarrhea. He is tachycardic with a third heart sound (an early diastolic sound just after the second heart sound) and crackles at both bases. Troponin is elevated and coronary angiography is normal. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Correct. Acute heart failure in an otherwise healthy young man with no cardiac history, one to two weeks after a flulike prodrome, with raised troponin and normal coronaries, is acute viral myocarditis.
Restrictive cardiomyopathy is rare, presents late with right-sided congestion, and follows infiltration, radiation or chemotherapy rather than a recent viral illness.
Stress (Takotsubo) cardiomyopathy follows an emotional or physical stressor, and 90% of cases are postmenopausal women. A viral prodrome in a young man points to myocarditis.
Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy is an inherited thickening of the septum with an outflow murmur and exertional syncope, not acute heart failure after a viral illness.

Deep vein thrombosis 3. Phlebitis a. Thrombophlebitis Septic thrombophlebitis 4. Arteriovenous fistula of the extremity a. Acquired (e.g. trauma, iatrogenic) b. Created (i.e. for hemodialysis) 5. Chronic venous insufficiency 6. Varicose veins
D.q: A 49-year-old man has a first proximal deep vein thrombosis with no surgery, trauma, hormone use, travel, cancer or other identifiable trigger, and no inherited disorder has been found. How long should anticoagulation continue?
opts: Six weeks is shorter than the minimum of three months required after any first venous thromboembolism. An unprovoked clot needs indefinite therapy.
Three months is the minimum for a clot provoked by a major transient risk factor such as surgery or major trauma. An unprovoked clot has no reversible trigger, so treatment continues beyond it.
Three to six months fits a clot provoked by a minor transient factor such as estrogen therapy, pregnancy, minor surgery or travel. An unprovoked clot has no such trigger and needs longer therapy.

Correct. A first venous thromboembolism with no identifiable risk factor is unprovoked, and its source, such as an undiscovered inherited clotting disorder, is unknown. Treatment therefore continues for an indefinite length of time.

D.io: Identify medical care strategies for pericardial disease in the lecture topic list for the following populations. 9. adult 10. elderly
D.q: An 84-year-old woman spent 9 days in the hospital for a large pericardial effusion that needed two procedures. She is now weak and needs help to walk. Besides cardiology and cardiothoracic surgery, which service is most appropriate before she goes home?
opts: Correct. Older adults are more likely to need rehabilitation after prolonged illness and procedures, which also carry higher morbidity and mortality at her age.
Genetic evaluation is not indicated for her pericardial disease. She needs rehabilitation.
Nephrology joins the follow-up when uremia causes the effusion, which nothing here suggests. Rehabilitation addresses her weakness and deconditioning.
Infectious disease follows an infectious cause such as tuberculosis, which nothing here suggests. Rehabilitation after her prolonged illness is the need.

D.topic: Differential diagnosis of a swollen leg

Deep vein thrombosis 3. Phlebitis a. Thrombophlebitis Septic thrombophlebitis 4. Arteriovenous fistula of the extremity a. Acquired (e.g. trauma, iatrogenic) b. Created (i.e. for hemodialysis) 5. Chronic venous insufficiency 6. Varicose veins
D.q: A 57-year-old man with knee osteoarthritis felt a sudden sharp pain behind the right knee while climbing stairs, followed by severe calf discomfort and swelling. Venous duplex ultrasound shows no thrombus. What is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: A calf muscle tear follows an inciting injury and may leave bruising at the ankle. Here the pain began behind the knee during ordinary activity, which fits a ruptured cyst better.

Correct. A ruptured popliteal (Baker) cyst produces severe, sudden calf discomfort that mimics deep vein thrombosis, and the ultrasound shows no clot. It is a standard item on the differential of a swollen calf.
Post-thrombotic syndrome is chronic venous insufficiency appearing 6 to 24 months after a clot, with slow-onset edema and skin change. A sudden calf event with no prior clot is not that.
Superficial thrombophlebitis gives a tender, indurated cord along a superficial vein with local redness. A sudden severe calf pain that began behind the knee is not a superficial vein process.

D.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following cardiomyopathies: 2. Restrictive cardiomyopathy 3. Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy 4. Dilated cardiomyopathy 5. Stress cardiomyopathy 6. Myocarditis
D.q: A 27-year-old woman with obstructive hypertrophic cardiomyopathy is examined by a student who hears a loud systolic murmur at the left sternal border. Respiration does not change it. Which bedside maneuver would soften her murmur?
opts: Standing decreases preload, which worsens outflow obstruction and makes the murmur of obstructive hypertrophic cardiomyopathy louder rather than softer.
The Valsalva maneuver decreases preload and increases the outflow obstruction, so it makes the murmur louder. Handgrip, squatting and leg raising soften it.

Correct. Anything that increases blood flow in the heart reduces outflow obstruction and softens the murmur. Handgrip raises afterload, and squatting or passive leg raising raise preload, so all three decrease the murmur.
Amyl nitrite decreases afterload, which increases outflow obstruction and makes the murmur louder. Increasing afterload with handgrip softens it.

D.q: A 67-year-old woman is recovering in hospital from stress cardiomyopathy that followed news of her son's serious illness. Her chest pain has resolved, and she asks whether her heart will stay damaged. Which answer about her prognosis is most accurate?
opts: Correct. Takotsubo is a transient regional systolic dysfunction, and most patients completely recover, which distinguishes its prognosis from the progressive cardiomyopathies.
The poorest prognosis among heart muscle diseases belongs to restrictive cardiomyopathy. Stress cardiomyopathy usually resolves completely.
Fifty percent mortality at five years describes symptomatic dilated cardiomyopathy. Most patients with stress cardiomyopathy recover completely.
The dysfunction in Takotsubo is transient, and most patients recover completely rather than progressing to chronic heart failure.

D.q: A 68-year-old man who smokes and has diabetes reports aching in both buttocks and hips after walking two blocks, relieved by about 10 minutes of rest. He also reports erectile dysfunction. Both femoral pulses are diminished. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Correct. Buttock and hip claudication points to the aortoiliac segment, and the triad of claudication, absent or diminished femoral pulses and erectile dysfunction is Leriche syndrome, the severe form of aortoiliac disease.
Spinal stenosis mimics claudication but brings numbness and weakness and is relieved only by sitting or leaning forward. It does not diminish the femoral pulses or cause this triad.
Tibial and peroneal disease produces foot claudication with normal femoral pulses. Buttock pain, erectile dysfunction and weak femoral pulses point to the aortoiliac segment.
Superficial femoral stenosis gives upper two-thirds calf claudication, the most common site. Buttock and hip pain with weak femoral pulses places the lesion higher, in the aortoiliac segment.

Correct. A pseudoaneurysm under 2 cm in diameter may undergo spontaneous thrombosis and regression, so watchful waiting is appropriate.
Heparin anticoagulates and would work against the thrombosis that seals a pseudoaneurysm. Under 2 cm the plan is to watch and wait.
Thrombolysis dissolves clot in acute limb ischemia. A small pseudoaneurysm is expected to seal by clotting, so it is watched.

D.q: What must follow chest or back pain in a patient with a known thoracic aortic aneurysm?
opts: Pain cannot be dismissed. Urgent imaging must rule out the aneurysm as its cause.
Stress testing is not the step named. The patient needs urgent imaging of the aneurysm.
Pain changes the urgency. It requires urgent imaging, not routine scheduled surveillance.
Correct. Chest or back pain with a known or suspected thoracic aortic aneurysm must undergo urgent imaging to rule out the aneurysm as the cause of the pain.

D.q: A 51-year-old woman with dilated, tortuous leg veins has a duplex ultrasound confirming superficial venous reflux. Which vein is most commonly involved in this condition?
opts: Correct. Varicose veins usually involve the superficial veins, and the great saphenous vein is the most commonly involved, with the short saphenous vein also affected.
The femoral vein is a deep vein, and varicose veins are a disease of the superficial system. The great saphenous vein is most commonly involved.
The short saphenous vein is also involved in varicose veins, but less often than the great saphenous vein, which is the most commonly affected.
The popliteal vein is a deep vein behind the knee. Superficial reflux most commonly involves the great saphenous vein.

D.q: A 70-year-old man presents with painful blue toes and palpable pedal pulses. On abdominal examination there is a pulsatile mass above the umbilicus. Which lesion is the likely source of his emboli?
opts: A femoral pseudoaneurysm follows catheterization and causes local pain from swelling. A pulsatile abdominal mass with blue toes indicates an abdominal aortic aneurysm.
Carotid plaque embolizes to the brain and retina, causing transient ischemic attack or stroke. Emboli to the toes with a pulsatile abdominal mass come from the aorta.
Dissection presents with sudden tearing chest pain from an intimal tear. The pulsatile abdominal mass here is an abdominal aortic aneurysm shedding emboli to the toes.
Correct. Atheroemboli originate from proximal atherosclerotic plaques, and an abdominal aortic aneurysm can itself shed emboli, producing blue toe syndrome as one of its embolic phenomena.

Paroxysmal supraventricular tachycardia
D.q: In sick sinus syndrome, a fast run that is irregularly irregular with no P waves alternates with pauses. Which rhythm is the fast run?
opts: Correct. An irregularly irregular fast rhythm with no P waves is atrial fibrillation, and in tachy-brady syndrome, the form of sick sinus syndrome in which fast and slow rhythms alternate, atrial fibrillation is the most common tachyarrhythmia.

Ventricular tachycardia can be the fast rhythm in a few patients, who then need a pacemaker with a defibrillator, but it is regular and wide; an irregularly irregular run without P waves is atrial fibrillation.
ruled out by a stated finding
Sinus tachycardia is regular, with a normal P wave before every QRS; in tachy-brady syndrome the fast rhythm comes from outside the failing sinus node, most commonly atrial fibrillation.
ruled out by a stated finding
Multifocal atrial tachycardia is irregular too, but every QRS has a P wave, in at least three shapes; a fast run with no P waves is atrial fibrillation, the usual fast rhythm of tachy-brady syndrome.
ruled out by a stated finding

D.q: A 65-year-old woman with a normal pulse examination and ankle-brachial index has had her venous ulcer heal after months of compression. She asks why it opened again after she bumped her leg. Which feature of a healed venous ulcer explains this?
opts: Correct. A venous ulcer heals with a thin scar that breaks down easily with minor trauma or increased leg edema, so recurrence is common without consistent compression.
A closed ulcer without signs of infection does not explain new breakdown. The healed area is a thin scar that opens with trauma or increased edema.
Lymphatic obstruction causes lymphedema, a different disorder. A healed venous ulcer reopens because its scar is thin and fragile.
Her pulses and ankle-brachial index are normal, so arterial supply is adequate. The scar itself is thin and breaks down with minor trauma or recurrent edema.

D.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following: 2. Acute endocarditis 3. Subacute endocarditis
D.q: A 76-year-old woman had a mechanical mitral valve placed 4 years ago. She has 5 weeks of low-grade fever and fatigue, and blood cultures are pending. Which organism is most likely in her prosthetic valve infection?
opts: Correct. Late prosthetic valve endocarditis is caused by viridans streptococci, while early infection (around surgery) is caused by coagulase-negative staphylococci and Staphylococcus aureus.
Gram-negative bacilli are uncommon causes of endocarditis. Late prosthetic valve infection is viridans streptococcal.
Staphylococcus epidermidis is the classic early prosthetic valve organism; 4 years out, viridans streptococci are expected.
Candida causes fungal endocarditis, mostly with immunocompromise or central lines; the late prosthetic valve organism is viridans streptococci.

Chronic venous insufficiency 6. Varicose veins
D.q: A 58-year-old man receiving chemotherapy for colon cancer comes to the emergency department with three days of left calf swelling that measures 4 cm more than the right, plus tenderness along the deep veins of the calf. He has no history of clots and nothing else explains his leg. The team debates whether to order a D-dimer or go straight to imaging. Using the Wells criteria, which is the best next step?
opts: Starting with a D-dimer is the path for low or moderate scores. With a high Wells score the D-dimer is skipped, because even a negative result would not exclude deep vein thrombosis and ultrasound is needed.
The ankle-brachial index screens for peripheral artery disease in arterial insufficiency. His swollen, tender calf points to venous thrombosis, so the test needed is venous duplex ultrasound.
Contrast ascending venography is the invasive gold standard but has been replaced by venous duplex ultrasound, which is noninvasive and is the imaging test ordered for a high score.

Correct. Active cancer, calf swelling over 3 cm and tenderness along the deep veins total 3 points, a high likelihood. A score of 3 or more skips the D-dimer and goes directly to venous duplex ultrasound of the leg.

Junctional rhythm i. QT prolongation
D.q: A 75-year-old man with complete heart block is stabilized with transcutaneous pacing in the emergency department. Which is the definitive treatment?
opts: An implantable cardioverter defibrillator shocks lethal ventricular rhythms. Complete block needs a permanent pacemaker.
Ablation destroys conduction tissue and is itself a named cause of complete block. The definitive treatment is a permanent pacemaker.
Correct. Transcutaneous pacing is the emergent bridge; the definitive treatment for complete (third-degree) atrioventricular block is a permanent pacemaker.
A beta blocker slows conduction further. Complete block is treated definitively with a permanent pacemaker.

D.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following pericardial disease: 2. Pericarditis 3. Acute 4. Recurrent 5. Constrictive pericarditis 6. Pericardial effusion 7. Cardiac tamponade
D.q: A 28-year-old man had a cold 10 days ago. He now has sharp, pleuritic (worse with a deep breath) substernal chest pain that is worse lying flat and eases when he leans forward. A pericardial friction rub (a scratchy, squeaking sound) is heard at the left sternal border, and the electrocardiogram shows widespread concave ST elevation with PR depression and ST depression in aVR. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Embolism can cause pleuritic pain, but not a friction rub with diffuse ST elevation and PR depression that improves on leaning forward.
An infarction gives convex ST elevation confined to one coronary territory with pressure-like pain, not diffuse concave elevation, PR depression and pain eased by leaning forward.
A pleural rub is tied to breathing and stops with breath-holding, and pleuritis does not produce widespread ST elevation with PR depression.

Correct. Sharp pleuritic, positional pain after a viral illness, a friction rub and widespread concave ST elevation with PR depression (reciprocal changes in aVR) meet well over two of the four diagnostic criteria for acute pericarditis.

Arterial thrombosis/embolism 3. Peripheral artery disease 4. Carotid artery disease 5. Aortic aneurysms 6. Aortic dissection
D.q: Where do atherosclerotic lesions most often form?
opts: At branch points and turbulent sites

Correct. Atherosclerotic lesions form at arterial bifurcations (branching) and at sites of increased turbulence, and they develop over many decades before causing stenosis, thrombosis or atheroemboli.
In the veins draining the lower legs
Atherosclerosis is an arterial disease of intermediate and large arteries. It forms at arterial branch points and sites of turbulence, not in leg veins.
In straight segments with laminar flow
Laminar flow along straight segments is the protected pattern. Lesions favor bifurcations and turbulent regions, where flow swirls against the wall.
In the smallest arterioles of the skin
Atherosclerosis affects intermediate and large arteries such as the coronary, carotid and femoral arteries and the aorta, not the skin's smallest arterioles.

D.q: A 52-year-old man with end-stage dilated cardiomyopathy is listed for cardiac transplantation, but his breathlessness and fatigue worsen despite full medical therapy and a biventricular defibrillator. Which device strategy fits his situation?
opts: Assist device as a bridge to transplant
Correct. A left ventricular assist device pumps blood from the left ventricle into the aorta. As bridge therapy it supports a patient awaiting transplantation or waiting for function to return.
A permanent pacemaker treats conduction disease such as nodal fibrosis in restrictive cardiomyopathy. It does not support the failing pump of end-stage dilated disease.
Destination therapy is for patients who are not candidates for transplantation. He is already listed, so the device would serve as a bridge to transplant instead.
Alcohol septal ablation thins an obstructing septum in hypertrophic cardiomyopathy. A dilated, failing ventricle needs mechanical support such as an assist device.

D.q: A 74-year-old man with heart failure has runs of 5 identical wide QRS beats on a Holter monitor. He has no symptoms during them. Which is the most appropriate management?
opts: Non-sustained ventricular tachycardia in and of itself is not an indication for a defibrillator. His underlying disease should be optimized.
Cardioversion is for sustained, unstable tachycardia. Brief silent runs are managed by optimizing underlying disease.
Correct. Asymptomatic non-sustained ventricular tachycardia is managed by optimizing treatment of the underlying cardiac comorbidities; it is not by itself an indication for a defibrillator.
Antiarrhythmics are kept for symptomatic episodes after other options. Silent runs call for optimizing his heart failure.

D.q: A 63-year-old man is diagnosed with a first proximal deep vein thrombosis five days after knee replacement under two hours of general anesthesia. His clot is attributed to the venous stasis and endothelial trauma of the Virchow triad, both from the surgery. What duration of anticoagulation is appropriate?
opts: Indefinite anticoagulation is for a first clot with no identifiable risk factor. His clot has a clear, reversible surgical cause, so open-ended treatment is not needed.

Correct. A clot provoked by a major transient, reversible risk factor, such as surgery under general anesthesia for more than 30 minutes, is treated for three months. Three months is also the minimum initial duration for any first venous thromboembolism.

Three to six months fits a clot provoked by a minor transient factor such as estrogen therapy, pregnancy, minor surgery or prolonged travel. Major surgery is a stronger reversible trigger, so three months suffices.
Six weeks falls short of the minimum. Every first venous thromboembolism, provoked or not, is treated for at least three months before the duration is reconsidered.

D.q: A 34-year-old woman has been hospitalized for four days receiving intravenous antibiotics through a peripheral catheter in her left forearm. She now has pain, redness and warmth along the course of the vein, and a firm, tender, palpable cord can be felt beneath the skin. She is afebrile, and the redness stays within the line of the vein. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Cellulitis is a diffuse skin infection with spreading redness, often with fever, and no discrete cord along a vein. A tender cord beneath a cannulated vein points to superficial thrombophlebitis instead.

Upper extremity deep vein thrombosis usually presents with limb swelling and arm discomfort from a deeper vein. A palpable cord with erythema tracking a superficial vein points to superficial thrombophlebitis.

Septic thrombophlebitis brings high fever, fluctuance or purulent drainage, with erythema extending well beyond the vein margin. She is afebrile with redness confined to the vein, so a sterile superficial process fits.

Correct. Tenderness, induration and erythema along a superficial vein, with an indurated palpable cord after recent catheter use, is superficial thrombophlebitis. Redness confined to the vein argues against infection.

D.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following cardiomyopathies: 2. Restrictive cardiomyopathy 3. Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy 4. Dilated cardiomyopathy 5. Stress cardiomyopathy 6. Myocarditis
D.q: A 19-year-old college athlete has exertional chest pain without coronary disease and a harsh systolic murmur at the left sternal border. Hypertension and aortic valve disease have been excluded. Which echocardiogram finding confirms the clinical diagnosis of hypertrophic cardiomyopathy?
opts: Mid and apical hypokinesis after a stressor is stress (Takotsubo) cardiomyopathy. Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy is confirmed by an unexplained wall of 1.5 cm or more.
Unexplained wall of 1.5 cm or more

Correct. The clinical diagnosis is confirmed when echocardiography shows unexplained left ventricular wall thickness of 1.5 cm or more anywhere in the wall, most often as asymmetric septal hypertrophy with a small cavity.
Dilated thin walls with low fraction
Dilated, thin walls with a reduced ejection fraction describe dilated cardiomyopathy. Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy has thick walls, a small cavity and a normal or high ejection fraction.
Pericardial thickening marks constrictive pericarditis and is shown on cardiac magnetic resonance imaging. The hypertrophic diagnosis rests on unexplained wall thickening.

D.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following pericardial disease: 2. Pericarditis 3. Acute 4. Recurrent 5. Constrictive pericarditis 6. Pericardial effusion 7. Cardiac tamponade
D.q: A 65-year-old woman with lung cancer has a moderate effusion, dyspnea and a blood pressure of 100/68. Her clinician measures her blood pressure through the respiratory cycle. Which result most supports tamponade?
opts: An unchanged pressure does not suggest tamponade, where pulsus paradoxus brings a 10 mmHg drop in blood pressure with inspiration.
Correct. Pulsus paradoxus, a 10 mmHg drop in blood pressure with inspiration, is a physical finding of both acute and subacute tamponade, along with an elevated jugular venous pressure.
Blood pressure drops, not rises, with inspiration in tamponade; pulsus paradoxus is a 10 mmHg drop in blood pressure with inspiration.
A 4 mmHg drop falls short of the 10 mmHg inspiratory drop in blood pressure that marks pulsus paradoxus in tamponade.

D.io: Identify medical care strategies for infective endocarditis for the following populations. 8. infant 9. child 10. adolescent 11. adult 12. elderly
D.q: A 2-month-old infant with a central line has poor feeding, fast breathing, tachycardia and a changing murmur. Blood cultures are positive and echocardiography shows a vegetation. Which complications are particularly common in infants because of septic emboli?
opts: Glomerulonephritis is an immunologic sign, not the listed infant complication of septic emboli.
Correct. Septic emboli are common in neonates and infants, producing osteomyelitis, meningitis or pneumonia, and neurologic signs such as seizures, hemiparesis and apnea.
Pediatric endocarditis causes less heart failure than adult disease; septic emboli are the infant problem.
Classic peripheral stigmata are considerably less common in children; infants' septic emboli cause osteomyelitis, meningitis or pneumonia.

D.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following pericardial disease: 2. Pericarditis 3. Acute 4. Recurrent 5. Constrictive pericarditis 6. Pericardial effusion 7. Cardiac tamponade
D.q: A 61-year-old woman with recurrent pericarditis over several years now has leg edema, ascites and an elevated jugular venous pressure. Constrictive pericarditis is suspected. Which echocardiogram finding would best support it?
opts: Right ventricular diastolic collapse is the echocardiographic sign of tamponade, from fluid under pressure, not constriction.
Asymmetric septal hypertrophy is hypertrophic cardiomyopathy. Constriction shows a septal bounce and a thick pericardium.
A dilated, poorly contracting ventricle is dilated cardiomyopathy; constriction keeps systolic function and restricts filling.
Septal bounce toward the left ventricle

Correct. Echocardiographic features of constriction are increased pericardial thickness, abnormal septal motion or bounce toward the left ventricle, pronounced respiratory variation in ventricular filling and moderate biatrial enlargement.

D.io: Identify medical care strategies for cardiomyopathies for the following populations. 8. adolescent 9. adult 10. elderly
D.q: Which cardiomyopathy strategy applies specifically to adolescents?
opts: Correct. For adolescents the strategies are genetic screening for hypertrophic cardiomyopathy and activity restriction for high-risk individuals.
Cautious use of diuretics and vasodilators
Cautious diuretics and vasodilators are an elderly strategy, tailored to comorbidity and frailty. Adolescents get hypertrophic cardiomyopathy screening.
Palliative care discussions in advanced stages are listed for the elderly. Adolescents get genetic screening for hypertrophic cardiomyopathy.
An assist device or transplant is considered in advanced adult cases. The adolescent strategy is genetic screening for hypertrophic cardiomyopathy.

D.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following pericardial disease: 2. Pericarditis 3. Acute 4. Recurrent 5. Constrictive pericarditis 6. Pericardial effusion 7. Cardiac tamponade
D.q: A 48-year-old man becomes hypotensive and short of breath an hour after a catheter procedure perforates his heart. Echocardiogram shows only a small pericardial effusion, estimated at about 150 mL, with right ventricular diastolic collapse. Which best explains why so little fluid has compromised him?
opts: A pericardium that stretches over time lets a chronic effusion grow large without tamponade; here the fluid arrived fast into an unstretched sac, so under 200 mL was enough.
There is no need to assume a measurement error; small, rapid effusions can cause tamponade.
Rapid filling of an unstretched sac
Correct. Acute effusions can produce tamponade with small amounts of fluid (under 200 mL) because the pericardium has no time to stretch, unlike chronic effusions that grow large over time.
Calcification belongs to constriction. Here the problem is rapid fluid entry into a normal, unstretched sac.

D.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following atrial and supraventricular dysrhythmias: a. Sinus arrhythmia b. Sinus bradycardia c. Sinus tachycardia d. Sick sinus syndrome e. Atrial premature beats f. Atrial flutter g. Atrial fibrillation h. Atrial tachycardia i. Paroxysmal supraventricular tachycardia
D.q: A 68-year-old man is brought in confused, with a blood pressure of 76/40. The monitor shows a slow, regular rhythm at 36 with a normal P wave before every narrow QRS. Which is the first-line treatment?
opts: A permanent pacemaker is definitive care for chronic symptomatic bradycardia; the acutely unstable patient first gets atropine, then temporary pacing.
Adenosine blocks the atrioventricular node to stop supraventricular tachycardia; in a slow, unstable rhythm it would deepen the bradycardia.

Correct. Acute, symptomatic, hemodynamically unstable sinus bradycardia is treated first with atropine; if it fails, a temporary pacemaker follows, and chronic symptomatic disease gets a permanent one.
Synchronized cardioversion is a timed shock for an unstable tachycardia with a pulse; unstable bradycardia is treated with atropine first.

E.io: Identify medical care strategies for cardiomyopathies for the following populations. 8. adolescent 9. adult 10. elderly
E.q: When are palliative care discussions raised for elderly patients with cardiomyopathy?
opts: They are explicitly part of elderly care. Palliative care discussions are held in the advanced stages of disease.
Palliative discussions are placed in the advanced stages rather than at the first encounter, once the disease has progressed.
Transplant is a curative-intent option in advanced adult disease; palliative discussions in the elderly come in advanced stages, not after transplant.
Correct. Palliative care discussions belong to the advanced stages in the elderly, alongside tailored therapy, cautious diuretics and vasodilators, and a focus on quality of life.

E.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following cardiomyopathies: 2. Restrictive cardiomyopathy 3. Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy 4. Dilated cardiomyopathy 5. Stress cardiomyopathy 6. Myocarditis
E.q: What is the most frequent presumed cause of myocarditis in developed countries?
opts: Correct. In developed countries viral infection is presumed to be the most frequent cause, including parvovirus B19, enteroviruses such as Coxsackie group B, adenoviruses and hepatitis C.
Lupus, rheumatoid arthritis and myasthenia gravis are causes, but the most frequent presumed cause in developed countries is viral infection.
Bacteria such as diphtheria, meningococcus and Mycoplasma can cause myocarditis, but viral infection is presumed most frequent in developed countries.
Penicillin, thiazide diuretics, tetracycline and methyldopa can cause myocarditis, but viral infection is presumed most frequent.

E.q: A 66-year-old woman with viridans streptococcal endocarditis had positive blood cultures on days 1 and 2 and her first negative culture on day 4. She asks how long her antibiotics will last. Which answer is most accurate?

Correct. Therapy is typically 4-6 weeks counted from the first negative culture, here day 4, because all bacteria in the vegetation must be killed.
The clock does not start at admission; it starts at the first negative blood culture, which here was day 4.

E.q: A 71-year-old woman with restrictive cardiomyopathy has fatigue and exercise intolerance along with leg edema, hepatomegaly and ascites, but her lungs are relatively clear. Which pattern of heart failure is expected to dominate in this condition?
opts: Left-sided failure brings pulmonary congestion, crackles and orthopnea to the fore. In restrictive cardiomyopathy right-sided failure often dominates instead.
Restrictive cardiomyopathy reduces output because stiff ventricles fill poorly. The dominant pattern is right-sided failure, not a high-output state.
Correct. Although filling pressures are raised in both ventricles, right heart failure is often more prominent and may dominate in restrictive cardiomyopathy, giving edema, hepatomegaly and ascites.
Systolic function is usually normal in restrictive cardiomyopathy; the problem is diastolic filling, and right-sided failure tends to dominate.

E.q: A 62-year-old man with dilated cardiomyopathy and an ejection fraction of 30% is in sinus rhythm, has native heart valves and has no thrombus on echocardiogram. His neighbor with heart failure takes a blood thinner, and he asks whether he should too. Which response about anticoagulation is most accurate?
opts: Needed by every dilated cardiomyopathy patient
Anticoagulation is not universal in dilated cardiomyopathy; it is limited to atrial fibrillation, artificial valves or a known mural thrombus, none of which he has.
Not needed in sinus rhythm without thrombus
Correct. In dilated cardiomyopathy anticoagulation is restricted to patients with atrial fibrillation, an artificial valve or a known mural thrombus. He has none of the three, so it is not indicated.
Needed only after a heart transplant is done
Transplantation is not an anticoagulation trigger in this list. Anticoagulation is kept for atrial fibrillation, artificial valves or a mural thrombus in the dilated ventricle.
Needed once ejection fraction falls below half
A low ejection fraction on its own is not the trigger. The listed indications are atrial fibrillation, an artificial valve and a known mural thrombus.

E.q: Which causes should be checked first in a patient with frequent premature ventricular contractions?
opts: High cholesterol and obesity are coronary risk factors, not the named causes to check. Hypoxemia and electrolyte imbalance (low potassium, low magnesium, high calcium) are the causes to look for first.
Dehydration and fever are not the named causes. Hypoxemia and electrolyte imbalances head the list for premature ventricular contractions.

Correct. Hypoxemia and electrolyte imbalances (hypokalemia, hypomagnesemia, hypercalcemia) are the main causes, so new frequent premature ventricular contractions call for checking oxygen and electrolytes.
Hypertension and diabetes drive degenerative conduction disease. Premature ventricular contractions come mainly from hypoxemia and electrolyte imbalance.

opts: Correct. Congenital fistulas are difficult to treat because the communications can be numerous, so they are managed conservatively with elastic support hose once peripheral artery disease is excluded. Embolization sometimes removes one.
Ligating each communication is impractical because the connections can be numerous. Conservative treatment with elastic support hose is the standard initial approach.
Surgical removal or size reduction suits an acquired fistula. Congenital fistulas have numerous communications, making excision difficult, so conservative care is used first.

E.q: Acute pericarditis is inflammation of the pericardial sac that lasts less than how long?
opts: Two to three days is far too short a cutoff. The acute label covers inflammation lasting up to 4 to 6 weeks before the incessant label applies.
Correct. Acute pericarditis is inflammation of the pericardial sac lasting less than 4 to 6 weeks; symptoms beyond that without remission are called incessant, and beyond 3 months chronic.
Three months is the line for chronic pericarditis, when symptoms persist beyond it. Acute pericarditis is the episode lasting under 4 to 6 weeks.
One year is not a pericarditis time frame at all. Acute means under 4 to 6 weeks, incessant runs to 3 months, and chronic is anything beyond 3 months.

E.q: A 62-year-old woman with suspected tamponade undergoes right heart catheterization before drainage. Which pressure finding is expected?
opts: Correct. Cardiac catheterization in tamponade shows equalization of pressures in all chambers of the heart, because the pericardial fluid under pressure dictates diastolic pressure throughout.
A gradient across the aortic valve
A transvalvular gradient indicates aortic stenosis, not tamponade, which equalizes pressures in all chambers.
An isolated high left atrial pressure
An isolated left atrial rise suggests left-sided failure or mitral disease; tamponade equalizes all chambers.
Right-sided pressures are high, not low, in tamponade, matching the distended neck veins.

E.q: Which electrolyte is given as an intravenous push and then as an infusion to break torsades de pointes?
opts: Phosphate plays no named role in torsades. Intravenous magnesium, then a magnesium infusion, is the treatment.
Low calcium is a cause of a long QT, yet calcium is not the treatment that breaks torsades. Magnesium is.
Low potassium is a cause of a long QT and should be corrected, but the drug that breaks torsades is intravenous magnesium.
Correct. In a conscious patient, intravenous magnesium breaks torsades de pointes, and more magnesium is then given as an infusion; it is the main treatment.

E.q: Which description fits a pericardial friction rub?
opts: Basal crackles that clear after the patient coughs
Crackles that clear with coughing come from the lungs. A pericardial friction rub is a scratchy, triphasic sound over the left sternal border.
Scratchy, triphasic, loudest at the left sternal border
Correct. The rub is classically triphasic with a superficial scratchy or squeaking quality, waxes and wanes, is loudest over the left sternal border and is best heard with the diaphragm.
Blowing holosystolic murmur radiating to the axilla
A blowing holosystolic murmur to the axilla is mitral regurgitation. The pericardial rub is scratchy or squeaking and triphasic.
Low-pitched diastolic rumble heard best at the apex
A low-pitched apical diastolic rumble is the murmur of mitral stenosis. A friction rub is a scratchy, triphasic sound at the left sternal border.

opts: Right bundle branch block gives an rsR' pattern in V1 to V3 and a slurred S wave in I and aVL, not a dominant S in V1.
First-degree block lengthens the PR interval with a narrow QRS. A QRS of 0.16 seconds with this lead pattern is left bundle branch block.

Correct. A QRS over 0.12 seconds with a dominant S wave in V1, a monophasic R in the lateral leads and absent Q waves in I, V5 and V6 is left bundle branch block; chronic hypertension is a named cause.

E.q: Which condition is a contraindication to anticoagulation for deep vein thrombosis?

Cancer raises clotting risk and is not a contraindication. Acute intracranial hemorrhage is.
A long flight is a risk factor for a clot, not a reason to withhold treatment. Acute intracranial hemorrhage is a contraindication.

Nothing else on the Wells criteria is present and no alternative diagnosis is as likely. What is his Wells score?
opts: One point undercounts. Each of his three positive items is worth 1 point, and none is offset by a likelier alternative diagnosis, which would subtract 2, so his total is three.
Two points would omit one positive item. The plaster immobilization, the calf swelling over 3 cm and the deep venous tenderness each score 1, so the total is three.

Correct. Recent plaster immobilization of the lower extremity, calf swelling over 3 cm and tenderness along the deep venous system are worth 1 point each, for 3. A score of 3 or more means high likelihood, so ultrasound is ordered.

A pacemaker is for slow rhythms; nodal reentry is a tachycardia managed with trigger avoidance and vagal maneuvers.

E.q: A 37-year-old man with acute pericarditis feels better after 5 days of ibuprofen and colchicine and plans to stop both medicines now. Which counseling point is most important?
opts: Finish the full course to prevent recurrence
Correct. Patient education stresses adherence to the full treatment course to prevent recurrence, which affects about 15 to 30% of patients, together with activity restriction and red-flag symptoms.
Stopping now is safe since the pain is gone
Pain relief at 5 days does not mean the inflammation has resolved; stopping early raises the risk of recurrence.
Switch to prednisone to finish faster
Prednisone is second line and does not shorten the course. Completing the prescribed regimen prevents recurrence.
Colchicine can stop; keep the ibuprofen
Colchicine is continued for about 3 months after a first episode because it reduces recurrence; it should not be dropped early.

Referral is appropriate for a pacemaker evaluation. The approach to avoid is simple observation of Mobitz type II.
A permanent pacemaker is the definitive treatment for Mobitz type II, so it should not be avoided; observation alone should be.
Checking for drugs that slow conduction is reasonable and not harmful. What should be avoided is observation without a pacemaker.

The drained volume does not set long-term prognosis; the underlying cause, here cancer, does.
Drainage has cured her for good

Venous duplex ultrasound of the arm

opts: Flutter shows sawtooth waves at an atrial rate of 250 or more; she has a normal P wave before each QRS at a rate near 110.
Focal atrial tachycardia has an abnormally shaped P wave from an ectopic focus and starts abruptly; her P waves are normal sinus P waves.

E.q: A 33-year-old woman eight weeks postpartum has mild calf aching and a low pretest probability of deep vein thrombosis. Her clinician orders a D-dimer. Which characteristic makes a negative result useful for excluding a clot?
opts: Testing whether a vein compresses is done with duplex ultrasound, not a blood test. D-dimer rules out disease through its sensitivity, not through any imaging feature.
D-dimer is a blood test that detects fibrin breakdown and cannot show a clot. Visualizing the thrombus is the job of venous duplex ultrasound.

Correct. D-dimer is sensitive but not specific, so a negative result in a low-likelihood patient effectively rules out deep vein thrombosis and pulmonary embolism. It cannot confirm a clot, since fibrinolysis has many causes.
D-dimer is not specific; many conditions raise it, so a positive result cannot confirm a clot. Its value as a rule-out test comes from high sensitivity.

E.q: A 65-year-old woman developed chest pain and dyspnea during a hurricane evacuation. She has ST elevation, an elevated troponin and B-type natriuretic peptide, and an echocardiogram showing akinesis of the left ventricular apex. Which test confirms stress cardiomyopathy?
opts: Exercise testing is inappropriate with active ST elevation and does not confirm the diagnosis. Cardiac catheterization with normal coronaries does.
Endomyocardial biopsy is the gold standard for myocarditis, not for stress cardiomyopathy. Catheterization with normal coronary arteries confirms Takotsubo.
Correct. The diagnosis of Takotsubo (stress) cardiomyopathy is confirmed with cardiac catheterization, which most often shows normal coronary arteries despite the infarct-like presentation.

E.q: A 70-year-old smoker has a painful, dry, punched-out ulcer at the tip of his second toe with minimal bleeding and surrounding black necrotic tissue. It started as a minor scrape months ago. Which complication is he at risk of?
opts: Correct. Ischemic skin ulcers fail to heal because blood supply cannot meet the demands of healing tissue; they sit at the most distal sites, are often ringed by dry gangrene, and can lead to osteomyelitis.
Aortic dissection is an intimal tear with a false lumen, presenting with tearing chest pain. The complication of a nonhealing ischemic toe ulcer is osteomyelitis.
A pseudoaneurysm follows arterial laceration, typically by a catheterization needle. A chronic ischemic toe ulcer threatens bone, leading to osteomyelitis.

E.q: An 81-year-old man with 3 months of weight loss presents with dyspnea and a large pericardial effusion. He has had no recent viral illness, chest surgery or radiation. Which etiology should be most strongly suspected?
opts: Rheumatic pancarditis follows streptococcal infection in younger patients and is not the concern here; malignancy is.
Correct. In older adults there is a higher index of suspicion for malignancy, especially with an effusion or tamponade, and his weight loss without a viral prodrome reinforces it.
Dressler syndrome follows myocardial infarction or cardiac surgery, which he has not had.
ruled out by a stated finding
Coxsackievirus is a classic cause of viral pericarditis and would usually follow a viral illness, which he has not had. Malignancy fits this older man.
ruled out by a stated finding

E.q: In tachy-brady syndrome, which tachyarrhythmia is most common?
opts: In tachy-brady syndrome the fast rhythm comes from outside the failing sinus node, most commonly atrial fibrillation, not a sinus tachycardia.
Atrial flutter is a fast atrial rhythm, but it is not the usual tachyarrhythmia of tachy-brady syndrome; atrial fibrillation is.
Ventricular tachycardia can be the fast rhythm in some patients, who then need a pacemaker with a defibrillator, but atrial fibrillation is the most common.
Correct. In tachy-brady syndrome a tachyarrhythmia, most commonly atrial fibrillation, alternates with symptomatic bradycardia or with offset pauses.

Correct. In stable supraventricular tachycardia, adenosine follows a failed vagal maneuver and may be repeated once; it may convert the rhythm or slow it enough to show P waves.
Atropine speeds the heart and treats unstable bradycardia; it would not stop a supraventricular tachycardia.
Magnesium breaks torsades de pointes; a stable narrow complex tachycardia gets adenosine after a failed vagal maneuver.

E.q: A 20-year-old man has just been diagnosed with hypertrophic cardiomyopathy on echocardiography. He has two younger sisters and a brother. His mother had unexplained sudden death at 44. Which step for his family is most appropriate?
opts: Most hypertrophic cardiomyopathy is inherited as an autosomal dominant trait, so his siblings each carry a real risk and should be evaluated.

Correct. Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy is mostly inherited in an autosomal dominant pattern, so one affected parent is enough to pass it on, and detection in a family member is a common reason evaluation of relatives begins.
Many patients are asymptomatic and are found only through family evaluation, and sudden death can be the first event. Relatives are evaluated whether or not they have symptoms.
Autosomal dominant inheritance affects both sexes, and males are affected more often than females. Every first-degree relative should be evaluated.

Magnesium is the treatment for torsades de pointes. Symptomatic non-sustained ventricular tachycardia starts with a beta blocker.

A urine culture looks for a urinary infection, which frothy urine does not suggest; frothy urine with edema points to nephrotic syndrome, so albumin and urine protein are checked.
Thyroid tests look for myxedema; his frothy urine and edema point to nephrotic syndrome.
Correct. Albumin and urine protein screen for nephrotic syndrome as a cause of pericardial effusion, alongside thyroid, rheumatologic, infectious and malignancy evaluation.

Correct. Atheroemboli of fibrin, platelets and cholesterol debris from proximal plaques lodge in small vessels of muscle and skin, causing blue toe syndrome with tenderness and pallor while distal pulses usually stay palpable.
Dry gangrene is hard, black, mummified tissue with clear demarcation. Tender blue toes with palpable pulses reflect small-vessel atheroemboli.
A thromboembolus occluding a limb artery produces a cold, pale leg with absent pulses. Palpable pulses with painful blue toes point to atheroembolism.

He now has a fever of 39.2 degrees Celsius, a tender cord along the vein, purulent drainage at the insertion site, and redness that extends several centimeters beyond the vein margin. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: A sterile superficial clot causes tenderness, induration and redness confined along the vein. Fever, purulent drainage and redness beyond the vein margin point to infection within the vein.
Correct. High fever, purulent drainage and erythema extending well beyond the margin of the vein after cannulation indicate infection within the vein, called suppurative or septic thrombophlebitis.
Upper extremity deep vein thrombosis presents mainly with limb swelling and discomfort. It does not produce purulent drainage at a catheter site or a fever with a tender superficial cord.
Cellulitis involves the skin without a source in the vein. Purulence at the insertion site with a tender cord and a prior catheter places the infection within the vein itself.

Clarithromycin is an appropriate oral option for a penicillin-allergic patient, even after anaphylaxis to penicillin.
Azithromycin is an appropriate oral option for a penicillin-allergic patient, even after anaphylaxis to penicillin.

Blood pressure matters only after surgery
Aggressive blood pressure control is part of management now, before any surgery. Hypertension is common in patients with thoracic aneurysm.
Correct. Management of a thoracic aortic aneurysm includes smoking cessation, beta-adrenergic blockers and aggressive blood pressure control, with surveillance imaging for his size.
Smoking matters only for leg disease

E.q: How is an aneurysm defined?
opts: Ten percent is far too small a change. The definition is localized dilation of more than 50% of normal diameter.
Any narrowing of the arterial lumen
Narrowing is stenosis, the opposite change. An aneurysm is a dilation greater than 50% of normal diameter.
Correct. An aneurysm is a pathologic dilation of a segment of a blood vessel, defined as localized dilation of an arterial segment greater than 50% of its normal diameter.
A tear through the intima alone
An intimal tear that opens a false lumen describes dissection. An aneurysm is dilation beyond 50% of normal diameter.

E.q: A perivalvular abscess that extends into the epicardium causes which complication?
opts: Correct. Extension of a perivalvular abscess into the epicardium causes pericarditis; extension into the upper ventricular septum interrupts conduction.
Atrial myxoma is a tumor in the differential diagnosis, not a complication of abscess spread. Epicardial extension causes pericarditis.
Heart block comes from extension into the upper ventricular septum, where the conduction system runs, not from epicardial spread.
Myocardial infarction is listed among the heart complications of endocarditis, but epicardial extension of a perivalvular abscess causes pericarditis.

E.q: A 72-year-old woman has sudden chest pain and diaphoresis an hour after learning she has lost her savings in a financial collapse. The electrocardiogram shows ST elevation and troponin is elevated. No catheterization has been done yet. Which is the most appropriate initial approach?
opts: Correct. Stress cardiomyopathy mimics acute coronary syndrome, and because there are no reliable early differences, evaluation and treatment follow the established protocols for acute coronary syndrome patients.
An emotional trigger does not exclude an acute coronary syndrome, and there are no reliable early features to tell them apart. She is managed on coronary protocols.
Nothing in her presentation calls for an inotrope. With no reliable early differences from a coronary event, she follows acute coronary syndrome protocols.
Alcohol septal ablation treats outflow obstruction in hypertrophic cardiomyopathy. ST elevation with chest pain is managed on acute coronary syndrome protocols.

E.q: A 58-year-old woman has a slow sinus rhythm at 38 six hours after an inferior myocardial infarction. She feels faint and her blood pressure is 80/50. Each narrow QRS has a normal P wave before it. Which drug should be given first?
opts: Diltiazem is a nondihydropyridine calcium channel blocker, another drug cause of bradycardia; it would worsen her hypotension and slow rate.
Correct. Acute, symptomatic, hemodynamically unstable sinus bradycardia, here from an infarction affecting the conduction tissue, is treated first with atropine, then a temporary pacemaker.
Metoprolol is a beta blocker, a listed cause of sinus bradycardia; it would slow her further.
Adenosine stops supraventricular tachycardia by blocking the atrioventricular node; it has no place in an unstable bradycardia.

opts: Antiphospholipid syndrome mimics endocarditis through thromboemboli and valve disease, not girdle myalgia.
Subacute endocarditis brings a new murmur and positive cultures in most patients; neither is present here.
ruled out by a stated finding
Atrial myxoma would give fever with a new murmur, such as a tumor plop; she has no murmur.
ruled out by a stated finding
Correct. Polymyalgia rheumatica sits in the differential of endocarditis because it causes myalgia with elevated inflammatory markers, but there is no murmur and cultures are negative.

E.q: A 61-year-old woman with long-standing diabetes describes a continuous burning sensation in both feet that is the same at rest and during exercise. Her pedal pulses are easily palpable. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Correct. Peripheral neuropathy, common in older patients with diabetes or alcoholism, causes a continuous burning sensation in the foot that is unaffected by exercise, unlike arterial claudication.
Arterial claudication is activity-related pain relieved by rest, with diminished pulses below the lesion. Constant burning unaffected by exercise with normal pulses is neuropathy.
Ischemic rest pain is worse with elevation and relieved by dangling the leg, and pulses are diminished. Her pulses are normal and position has no effect.
Spinal stenosis gives claudication-like pain with walking, relieved by sitting or leaning forward. Burning that is constant and unaffected by exercise is neuropathy.

opts: Older age raises atrial fibrillation risk but does not make a presentation an emergency; severe heart failure does.
An irregularly irregular pulse defines atrial fibrillation and is not itself the emergency.
Correct. Medical emergencies from atrial fibrillation include severe heart failure (pulmonary edema, hypotension) and atrial fibrillation with an acute myocardial infarction.
A rate above 100 is rapid ventricular response, which needs rate control but is not by itself the listed emergency.

E.q: A 67-year-old woman with hypertension has an acute aortic dissection with severe tearing chest pain and a blood pressure of 176/100. Which intravenous medication should be started first to lower her pressure?
opts: Cilostazol is an oral antiplatelet for claudication. Acute dissection is treated by lowering pressure and heart rate, starting with a beta blocker such as esmolol.

Correct. A beta blocker such as esmolol is given first, lowering heart rate and shear force to bring systolic pressure to 100 to 120 mmHg; a vasodilator such as nitroprusside is added only if pressure stays high.
Alteplase is the thrombolytic for catheter-directed treatment of acute limb ischemia. Dissection needs pressure reduction, starting with a beta blocker such as esmolol.
Heparin anticoagulates acute limb ischemia. The dissection needs its blood pressure and heart rate lowered, starting with a beta blocker such as esmolol.

E.q: A 59-year-old man with obstructive hypertrophic cardiomyopathy has just undergone alcohol septal ablation, in which alcohol is injected through a catheter into a septal branch of the coronary artery. He asks when he can expect his symptoms to improve. Which answer is most accurate?
opts: Never; it is a diagnostic test
Alcohol septal ablation is a treatment for outflow obstruction, not a diagnostic test. The septum thins over months after the therapeutic infarction.
A repeat procedure is not routine; the effect develops over months as the infarcted septal muscle thins. Reintervention is needed in a minority of patients.
Over months as the septum thins
Correct. Alcohol septal ablation induces a therapeutic infarction of the proximal septum, and it takes months for the septum to thin and the outflow obstruction to ease.
The ablation creates a controlled infarction of septal muscle, and the benefit comes as the septum thins, which takes months rather than minutes.

E.q: A 55-year-old man has 3 days of fever to 40.0 °C (104.0 °F), rigors and a new murmur, and he looks toxic. Which organism is a classic cause of this tempo of infective endocarditis?
opts: Coagulase-negative staphylococci are listed with the subacute organisms and with early prosthetic valve infection; a classic acute organism is Staphylococcus aureus.
Viridans streptococci cause subacute disease with low fevers over weeks, not a toxic course over 3 days.
Correct. An abrupt, toxic, high-fever course is acute endocarditis, caused by virulent organisms such as Staphylococcus aureus and beta-hemolytic streptococci.
The HACEK (Haemophilus, Aggregatibacter, Cardiobacterium, Eikenella, Kingella) group causes subacute endocarditis, not the acute toxic form.

E.q: An 80-year-old man has an incidental finding on a preoperative electrocardiogram: a constant PR interval in conducted beats with occasional P waves that are not followed by a QRS complex, and no PR lengthening before the dropped beats. He has no symptoms. Which is the most appropriate next step?
opts: Repeat the tracing in a year
Waiting ignores the unpredictable progression of Mobitz type II to complete heart block and sudden death. A pacemaker is indicated.

Correct. Mobitz type II is considered dangerous even without symptoms, because of unpredictable progression to complete block and a poor prognosis, so the definitive treatment is a permanent pacemaker.
Reassurance suits silent first-degree or Mobitz type I block. Mobitz type II needs a permanent pacemaker even without symptoms.
A beta blocker slows atrioventricular conduction and could worsen the block. Mobitz type II is treated with a permanent pacemaker.

E.q: A 59-year-old man in ventricular fibrillation arrest is shocked several times, and his rhythm changes to a flat line with no electrical activity in two leads. What does this change mean for his outlook?
opts: A flat line is not a successful conversion; there is no organized activity. It signals a much worse prognosis.
Asystole carries a poorer prognosis than ventricular fibrillation, not a better one.
The change matters: asystole is a poor-prognosis rhythm, whereas fibrillation has the best prognosis of the arrest rhythms.
Correct. Ventricular tachycardia and fibrillation have the best prognosis of the arrest rhythms; asystole has a poor prognosis and is usually an end-of-life rhythm.

E.q: A 29-year-old woman who delivered a healthy baby three months ago now has breathlessness on exertion, orthopnea (breathlessness lying flat) and swollen ankles. She had no heart disease before pregnancy. Echocardiogram shows a dilated left ventricle with an ejection fraction of 30%. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy is an inherited thickening of the septum with a small cavity and a normal ejection fraction. A dilated ventricle three months postpartum fits peripartum disease.

Restrictive cardiomyopathy has stiff walls, a near-normal cavity and big atria, often after radiation or infiltrative disease. A newly dilated, weak ventricle after delivery is peripartum cardiomyopathy.

Stress (Takotsubo) cardiomyopathy follows an emotional or physical stressor, mostly in postmenopausal women, and causes transient mid and apical hypokinesis rather than a dilated ventricle after pregnancy.
Correct. Peripartum cardiomyopathy is a rare form of dilated cardiomyopathy that develops in the last trimester of pregnancy or within the first six months after delivery, as it has here.

E.q: An 80-year-old man is found on the floor two days after collapsing. His right leg has profound sensory loss, paralysis with rigid muscles, and no arterial or venous Doppler signal. Which is the most appropriate next step?
opts: Clot removal is for limbs that can still be saved. Profound sensory loss, paralysis and absent venous signals mark an irreversible limb that needs major amputation.
Thrombolysis can restore flow to a salvageable limb of under 14 days. This limb is irreversibly damaged, and major amputation is needed regardless of therapy.
Imaging suits viable and marginally threatened limbs. For an irreversibly damaged limb, vascular imaging is generally not immediately needed; the limb requires amputation.

Correct. An irreversibly ischemic limb has major tissue loss or permanent nerve damage, profound sensory loss, paralysis and inaudible arterial and venous signals; nonviable limbs require major amputation whatever therapy is used.

opts: Age alone is not an indication. Mobitz type I is usually asymptomatic and needs no treatment; a pacemaker is considered once the block causes symptoms.
Dropped beats are the defining pattern of Mobitz type I, often with increased vagal tone, and need no treatment by themselves. Symptoms are what make her a pacemaker candidate.

Pyuria belongs to the expected urinalysis (with hematuria and proteinuria) but is not a Duke criterion; the immunologic criterion names rheumatoid factor.

E.q: A 32-year-old woman who is 34 weeks pregnant sits in a car for nine hours and develops left calf swelling and pain. Her pregnancy supplies a hypercoagulable state and the long ride supplies venous stasis. Which additional component would complete the Virchow triad?
opts: Correct. The Virchow triad is venous stasis, hypercoagulable state and endothelial trauma. Pregnancy and the car ride supply two components, so the missing one is injury to the vein wall, as from trauma, surgery, burns or injection.
Pregnancy already supplies the hypercoagulable state by raising clotting tendency, so it is present rather than missing. The component still absent is endothelial trauma.
Venous stasis is already present from nine hours of sitting still, so it cannot be the additional component. The one still missing is endothelial trauma, injury to the vessel wall.
Arterial thrombosis is a clot in an artery and is not a component of the Virchow triad. The venous component still absent in this scenario is endothelial trauma.

E.q: How is hemodynamically stable atrial flutter treated first?
opts: Ablation is the definitive management of flutter, chosen for recurrence rather than as the first step; a stable patient starts with rate control using a beta blocker or calcium channel blocker.
Correct. Stable atrial flutter is rate-controlled with a beta blocker or calcium channel blocker; an unstable patient gets synchronized cardioversion.
Adenosine is used for supraventricular tachycardia; stable flutter is rate-controlled with a beta blocker or calcium channel blocker.
Synchronized cardioversion is for unstable flutter; the stable patient starts with rate control.

E.q: A 24-year-old man whose Wolff-Parkinson-White was found on a school electrocardiogram presents with palpitations. The rhythm is irregular and wide-complex, at rates up to 260, with varying delta waves (slurred upstrokes). He is alert with a blood pressure of 118/74. Which drug is the most appropriate treatment?
opts: Magnesium breaks torsades de pointes, a polymorphic ventricular tachycardia with a long QT, not pre-excited atrial fibrillation.
Atropine speeds conduction and is for unstable bradycardia; it would accelerate a pre-excited tachycardia.
Adenosine is contraindicated here: it blocks only the normal node and lets the accessory pathway carry the fibrillation.
Correct. Irregular, wide, very fast complexes in a patient with Wolff-Parkinson-White are pre-excited atrial fibrillation, treated with intravenous procainamide; adenosine must never be used.

E.q: A 68-year-old man has had 6 weeks of low-grade fever and weight loss and has a new murmur. Subacute endocarditis is suspected. Which complete blood count finding is most likely?
opts: Correct. The complete blood count often shows leukocytosis and anemia of chronic disease with a normal mean corpuscular volume (normocytic).
Small red cells suggest iron deficiency, not the anemia of chronic disease, which is normocytic.
Eosinophilia points to allergy or parasites, not endocarditis; expect leukocytosis with a normocytic anemia of chronic disease.
Chronic infection lowers, not raises, the red cell mass; expect a normocytic anemia.

E.q: A 31-year-old man was treated for acute pericarditis 3 months ago and has been symptom-free for 6 weeks. His sharp, positional chest pain has now returned with a friction rub (a scratchy, squeaking sound). C-reactive protein is mildly raised. Which regimen is most appropriate?
opts: Prednisone alone is not the recurrence regimen; when used it is given with colchicine. Anti-inflammatory plus colchicine for 6 months or more comes first.
Ibuprofen with colchicine, stopped at 2 weeks
Two weeks of colchicine is far too short after a recurrence; the course is 6 months or more.
Anti-interleukin-1 therapy is for colchicine-resistant or steroid-dependent recurrence with a strong inflammatory phenotype, not a first recurrence.
Ibuprofen with colchicine for 6 months or more

Correct. This is a first recurrence, symptoms returning after a symptom-free interval of 4 to 6 weeks or longer, treated with a nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug plus colchicine for 6 months or more.
